kingdom-of-airgialla.t: Confederation of mid-Ulster peoples bound to the Uí Néill as hostage-givers, which survived under the MacMahons as Oriel until the settlement of Monaghan in 1591.
kingdom-of-airgialla.o: Airgialla means 'hostage-givers', and the name describes a group of peoples in mid-Ulster, in modern Armagh, Monaghan, Tyrone, Fermanagh and Louth, who owed hostages and military service to the Uí Néill. Tradition says the Three Collas destroyed Emain Macha, the royal centre of the Ulaid, and settled their descendants in the conquered land.
kingdom-of-airgialla.r: Airgialla was a federation of many small kingdoms, such as the Uí Chremthainn and the Uí Méith, under an over-king. Its people held the lands around Armagh, whose church became the primatial see of Ireland. In the 12th century Donnchad Ua Cerbaill, king of Airgialla, extended his realm into Louth and founded Mellifont Abbey in 1142, the first Cistercian house in Ireland.
kingdom-of-airgialla.e: Anglo-Norman settlement took Louth, and the MacMahons, Mac Mathghamhna, became rulers of the remaining kingdom, known in English as Oriel, centred on Monaghan. After the execution of Hugh Roe MacMahon in 1590, the English divided the lordship among MacMahon chiefs in 1591, creating County Monaghan.
kingdom-of-airgialla.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-ceredigion.t: Early Welsh kingdom on Cardigan Bay, named after its legendary founder Ceredig, which grew into Seisyllwg in the 8th century.
kingdom-of-ceredigion.o: Welsh tradition says the kingdom was founded by Ceredig, a son of Cunedda, who came from the north to drive Irish settlers out of Wales in the 5th century, and that the land took its name from him. This story was recorded centuries later and is regarded with caution by historians, but Ceredigion as a district between the Dyfi and the Teifi is ancient.
kingdom-of-ceredigion.r: Little is known of its rulers before the 8th century beyond genealogies. The kingdom covered the coastal lowlands and hills of modern Ceredigion, a region of small farms and cattle-rearing, and its church centres included Llanbadarn Fawr, associated with St Padarn, which became one of the leading monasteries of Wales.
kingdom-of-ceredigion.e: Around 730 its king Seisyll ap Clydog conquered the neighbouring Kingdom of Ystrad Tywi, creating an enlarged realm known as Seisyllwg. This later passed to Hywel Dda and became part of Deheubarth. The name survives in the modern county of Ceredigion.

kydonia.t: Leading city of western Crete for much of antiquity, a rival of Knossos and Gortyn, on the site of modern Chania.
kydonia.o: Kydonia stood on a Minoan site on the north-west coast of Crete. Herodotus records that Samian exiles fleeing Polycrates settled there in 524 BCE and built temples, before Aeginetans defeated them in 519 BCE and settled the city in their turn. By the classical period it was an independent Cretan polis named after its legendary founder Kydon.
kydonia.r: Kydonia was governed, like other Cretan cities, by annual officials called kosmoi and a council of elders, with a warrior aristocracy and dependent rural labourers. It struck silver coins, traded across the Aegean and supplied mercenaries, including famous archers. In the Hellenistic period it fought repeated wars with Knossos, Gortyn and Polyrrhenia.
kydonia.e: Rome intervened in Crete during the wars against the Cretan pirates. Quintus Caecilius Metellus besieged and took Kydonia in 69 BCE on his way to conquering the island, which became part of the province of Crete and Cyrene. Kydonia remained a free city under Rome and survives as Chania.

kamiros.t: Farming city on the west coast of Rhodes, one of the island's three ancient cities, whose terraced streets survive in remarkable condition.
kamiros.o: Kamiros was settled by Dorian Greeks in the early Iron Age on a slope above the west coast of Rhodes, facing Anatolia across the sea. It was one of the three Rhodian cities, with Lindos and Ialysos, and a member of the Dorian Hexapolis.
kamiros.r: Unlike Lindos, Kamiros relied mainly on farming of grain, figs, olives and wine. Its cemeteries have yielded rich finds of Archaic pottery and jewellery, giving its name to the 'Kamiran' style of East Greek ware. The city fell under the Achaemenid Empire and then belonged to the Delian League. Its acropolis held a temple of Athena Kameiras.
kamiros.e: In 408 BCE Kamiros joined Lindos and Ialysos to found the city of Rhodes and lost its political independence. It continued as a town; after earthquakes it was rebuilt in the Hellenistic period, and its houses and cistern can still be seen.
kamiros.re: Greek religion; cult of Athena Kameiras

kingdom-of-amathus.t: Cypriot kingdom on the south coast that kept the island's pre-Greek Eteocypriot language alive into the 4th century BCE.
kingdom-of-amathus.o: Amathus was founded c. 1050 BCE on a hill near modern Limassol. Ancient writers regarded its people as autochthonous Cypriots, and the city preserved the Eteocypriot language, written in the Cypriot syllabary, alongside Greek. It also had close links with Phoenicia, and its rulers paid tribute to Assyria in the 7th century BCE.
kingdom-of-amathus.r: The acropolis held a palace and a major sanctuary of the Cypriot goddess later called Aphrodite, with a giant stone vase now in the Louvre. The kingdom grew rich from copper and agriculture. It was loyal to Persia: in 498 BCE it refused to join the revolt led by Onesilus of Salamis and was besieged.
kingdom-of-amathus.e: King Androcles sent ships to help Alexander the Great at Tyre in 332 BCE. The monarchy was ended under Ptolemy I c. 312 BCE, and Amathus continued as a city under the Ptolemaic Empire and Rome. It declined after the 7th century CE and was abandoned.

kingdom-of-the-rugians.t: A small East Germanic kingdom north of the Danube in Lower Austria, known chiefly from the Life of Saint Severinus and destroyed by Odoacer in 487.
kingdom-of-the-rugians.o: The Rugii originally lived on the Baltic coast, where Tacitus places them. After migrating south and serving under the Huns, they settled after Attila's death in 453 on the north bank of the Danube opposite the Roman province of Noricum, in the area later called Rugiland, in modern Lower Austria.
kingdom-of-the-rugians.r: The Rugian kings were Arian Christians who dominated the remaining Roman towns of Noricum Ripense, collecting tribute and controlling trade across the Danube. Eugippius' Life of Saint Severinus portrays King Flaccitheus, his son Feletheus and the harsh Queen Giso, whom the saint rebuked. Their power depended on balancing Ostrogoths, Heruli and the Roman population.
kingdom-of-the-rugians.e: In 487 Odoacer, ruler of Italy, attacked Rugiland and captured Feletheus and Giso; in 488 his brother crushed their son Fredericus, and the Roman population of Noricum was evacuated to Italy. Surviving Rugians joined Theodoric's Ostrogoths and went with them to Italy, keeping a separate identity there into the 540s.

kingdom-of-the-franks.t: The Frankish realm founded by Clovis, the most lasting of the barbarian kingdoms and the common ancestor of France and Germany.
kingdom-of-the-franks.o: Clovis succeeded his father Childeric I as king of the Salian Franks at Tournai in 481. He destroyed the Domain of Soissons in 486, defeated the Alemanni, accepted Catholic baptism at Reims and in 507 crushed the Visigothic Kingdom at Vouillé, taking Aquitaine. He made Paris his capital and absorbed the other Frankish kingdoms.
kingdom-of-the-franks.r: The Merovingian kings divided the realm among their sons as private inheritance, creating Austrasia, Neustria and Burgundy. Gallo-Roman bishops, counts and a Frankish warrior aristocracy ran it together. From the 7th century real power passed to the mayors of the palace, and Charles Martel halted an Umayyad army near Tours in 732.
kingdom-of-the-franks.e: In 751 Pippin the Short deposed the last Merovingian, Childeric III, and became king. His son Charlemagne conquered Saxony and Lombard Italy and was crowned emperor in 800, ruling the Carolingian Empire. In 843 the Treaty of Verdun split the realm into West Francia, Middle Francia and East Francia.

kingdom-of-asturias.t: The first Christian kingdom in Iberia after the Muslim conquest, born at Covadonga and seen as the cradle of the Reconquista.
kingdom-of-asturias.o: After 711 the Visigothic noble Pelagius led a revolt in the mountains of Asturias and defeated a Muslim force at Covadonga, traditionally in 718 or 722. His small realm, based at Cangas de Onís, grew under Alfonso I, son of Duke Peter of the Duchy of Cantabria, who raided the Douro valley and absorbed Cantabria.
kingdom-of-asturias.r: Alfonso II the Chaste made Oviedo the capital and modelled his court on the Visigothic kingdom of Toledo. Under him the tomb of St James was proclaimed at Compostela, starting a great pilgrimage. Ramiro I built the pre-Romanesque churches of Monte Naranco. Alfonso III the Great resettled the Douro frontier, taking Porto in 868 and Coimbra in 878, and sponsored chronicles of a Gothic restoration.
kingdom-of-asturias.e: In 910 Alfonso III was deposed by his sons, who divided the realm into León, Galicia and Asturias. With Fruela II's death in 924 the court settled at León, and the Kingdom of Asturias gave way to the Kingdom of León.

kingdom-of-sussex.t: The kingdom of the South Saxons on the English Channel coast, among the earliest Anglo-Saxon realms and the last major one to accept Christianity.
kingdom-of-sussex.o: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says that Aelle and his three sons landed in 477 and fought the Britons near the shore, later storming the Roman fort of Anderitum (Pevensey) in 491. Bede names Aelle as the first overlord of the southern English. Settlement was hemmed in by the dense Weald forest, which isolated the kingdom from its neighbours.
kingdom-of-sussex.r: Sussex was small and inward-looking, with a farming economy on the coastal plain and the chalk downs. Its kings often stood under Mercian or West Saxon overlordship. Paganism lasted until Wilfrid of York converted the South Saxons in the 680s, founding a monastery and bishopric at Selsey on land given by King Aethelwealh. Several kings sometimes ruled at once.
kingdom-of-sussex.e: Caedwalla of Wessex overran Sussex in the 680s, and in the 8th century it fell under Offa of Mercia. After Ecgberht's victory at Ellendun in 825, Sussex submitted to the Kingdom of Wessex and became a shire. The name survives in the modern counties of East and West Sussex.

kingdom-of-aragon.t: The Pyrenean kingdom that conquered the Ebro valley, joined Catalonia to form the Crown of Aragon and kept its own laws until 1707.
kingdom-of-aragon.o: Aragon began as a small Carolingian-era county around Jaca. In 1035 Sancho III of Navarre left it to his son Ramiro I, who ruled as king in practice. His heirs Sancho Ramírez and Peter I expanded south, taking Huesca in 1096, and Alfonso I the Battler captured Zaragoza in 1118.
kingdom-of-aragon.r: The kingdom developed strong traditions of noble privilege: its Cortes, its fueros and the Justicia de Aragón, a judge who guarded the laws even against the king. Its economy rested on Ebro valley farming, wool and the many Muslim farmers, later called mudéjares and Moriscos, who stayed on the land. Zaragoza became its capital.
kingdom-of-aragon.e: The marriage of Petronila to Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona created the Crown of Aragon. Aragon kept its institutions under Habsburg Spain until Philip V abolished them by the Nueva Planta decrees of 1707 after the War of the Spanish Succession.

kingdom-of-brycheiniog.t: Welsh kingdom of the Usk valley, founded according to legend by the Irish-descended Brychan, whose royal crannog at Llangorse was stormed by the Mercians in 916.
kingdom-of-brycheiniog.o: Brycheiniog took its name from Brychan, a 5th-century ruler of Irish and British descent whose many saintly children are celebrated in Welsh and Cornish tradition. Ogham-inscribed stones in the region support Irish settlement in the post-Roman period. The kingdom occupied the upper Usk valley and the uplands around modern Brecon.
kingdom-of-brycheiniog.r: Its kings were often under pressure from larger neighbours. Asser records that Elisedd ap Tewdwr submitted to Alfred of Wessex in the 880s. The royal crannog on Llangorse Lake, an artificial island built in the 890s, is the only one known in Wales; in 916 the Mercians under Æthelflæd attacked it and carried off the king's wife. Tewdwr ab Elisedd later witnessed English royal charters.
kingdom-of-brycheiniog.e: Brycheiniog lost its independence in the 11th century, coming under the rulers of Deheubarth and Morgannwg. In 1093 the Norman Bernard de Neufmarché defeated and killed Rhys ap Tewdwr near Brecon and created the Norman lordship of Brecknock, which later became the county of Brecknockshire.

kingdom-of-rhos.t: Early kingdom of the north Welsh coast east of the Conwy, guarded by the fortress of Deganwy, which became a cantref of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-rhos.o: Rhos lay between the River Conwy and the Clwydian hills, on the coast of modern Conwy county. Welsh tradition linked it with the sons of Cunedda, and in the 6th century Gildas denounced Cuneglasus, often identified as a king of Rhos, as the charioteer of the Bear's Stronghold, possibly the hillfort of Bryn Euryn near Colwyn Bay.
kingdom-of-rhos.r: The fortress of Deganwy, on twin hills above the Conwy estuary, was associated with Maelgwn Gwynedd and with the rulers of Rhos, and excavation has found imported Mediterranean pottery of the 5th and 6th centuries. The kingdom was closely tied to the Kingdom of Gwynedd and its kings were probably a junior branch of Maelgwn's dynasty.
kingdom-of-rhos.e: In 822 the Mercians destroyed Deganwy and took Rhos for a time. Rhos was later firmly part of the Kingdom of Gwynedd as a cantref of the Perfeddwlad, contested with English kings, until the conquest of 1283.

kingdom-of-fortriu.t: The leading Pictish kingdom, whose kings dominated northern Britain in the 7th to 9th centuries and whose heartland is now placed around Moray.
kingdom-of-fortriu.o: Fortriu takes its name from the Verturiones, listed by Ammianus Marcellinus in the 360s as one of the two main peoples of the Picts. In early Irish annals 'king of Fortriu' became the title of the most powerful Pictish rulers. Long located in Strathearn, it is now usually placed around Moray and Easter Ross, following work by Alex Woolf.
kingdom-of-fortriu.r: Kings of Fortriu built an over-kingship across Pictland. Bridei son of Beli destroyed the Northumbrian army at Dun Nechtain in 685, ending English dominance in the north. Óengus son of Fergus, from 729 to 761, defeated rivals and even campaigned against Dál Riata and Strathclyde. Major centres included the fortress of Burghead and the monastery of Portmahomack. Later kings such as Constantín son of Fergus also ruled Dál Riata.
kingdom-of-fortriu.e: In 839 a Viking army killed the king of Fortriu, Eóganán, with many nobles. In the aftermath Cináed mac Ailpín seized power, and Fortriu merged into the Gaelic kingdom of Alba around 900. The region later re-emerged as the province of Moray.

kingdom-of-tamassos.t: Inland Cypriot kingdom built on rich copper mines, whose last king sold his realm to the king of Kition for fifty talents.
kingdom-of-tamassos.o: Tamassos lay in the Pediaios valley at the foot of the copper-rich Troodos mountains and was settled from the Bronze Age. Its copper may be the 'Temese' of Homer's Odyssey. By the 7th century BCE it was an independent kingdom; its king Admetus appears among the Cypriot rulers listed by Esarhaddon of Assyria.
kingdom-of-tamassos.r: The kingdom's wealth came from copper mining and smelting. Its royal tombs of the 6th century BCE are built of fine ashlar masonry imitating wooden houses, and a sanctuary of Apollo and the Mother of the Gods has yielded much sculpture. Tamassos used Greek and Phoenician alongside each other.
kingdom-of-tamassos.e: In the 4th century BCE King Pasicyprus sold Tamassos to Pumiyaton of the Kingdom of Kition for fifty talents. Alexander the Great later gave it to the king of Salamis. Tamassos survived as a town under Ptolemaic and Roman rule.

kingdom-of-surrey.t: A short-lived Saxon territory south of the Thames whose name, the 'southern district', survives as the county of Surrey.
kingdom-of-surrey.o: Surrey, Suthrige, probably began as the southern part of a larger Middle Saxon territory on both sides of the Thames. In the 7th century it lay between Kent, Wessex, Sussex and Mercia and was ruled by local leaders under one or another of them.
kingdom-of-surrey.r: The only known ruler is Frithuwold, a sub-king under Wulfhere of the Kingdom of Mercia, who around 672 to 674 endowed Chertsey Abbey, founded by Bishop Eorcenwald. The charter shows estates, minsters and Mercian overlordship but no independent dynasty.
kingdom-of-surrey.e: Surrey never had a lasting royal line. Control passed between Mercia and Wessex, and in the 9th century it became a West Saxon shire, keeping its name and much of its boundary.

kingdom-of-the-suebi.t: A Germanic kingdom that ruled Gallaecia from Braga for over 170 years, one of the first barbarian realms in the former Roman West.
kingdom-of-the-suebi.o: The Suebi crossed the Rhine in 406 with the Vandals and Alans and entered Hispania in 409. In 411 they received lands in Gallaecia under their king Hermeric. After the Vandals left for Africa in 429, Rechila expanded south, taking Emerita Augusta in 439 and Seville in 441.
kingdom-of-the-suebi.r: The kingdom was centred on Bracara Augusta and ruled a Hispano-Roman majority through bishops and local elites. Rechiar became the first Catholic Germanic king around 448 and minted silver coins, but was defeated and killed by the Visigoth Theodoric II in 456. The Suebi later turned Arian, then returned to Catholicism under Martin of Braga's influence around 560. The Councils of Braga of 561 and 572 organised the church.
kingdom-of-the-suebi.e: King Miro was drawn into Visigothic conflicts and died in 583. In 585 the Visigothic king Leovigild overthrew the usurper Andeca and annexed the kingdom, ending Suebic rule. Its territory shaped the later Kingdom of Galicia.

kingdom-of-york.t: The Viking kingdom centred on Jorvik, a prosperous Anglo-Scandinavian town whose kings were often also rulers of Dublin.
kingdom-of-york.o: The Great Heathen Army captured York in 866 to 867, and in 876 Halfdan shared out the land of Northumbria south of the Tees among his followers. Danish kings ruled from York, with Guthfrith in the 880s accepting Christianity. Early in the 10th century the Norse dynasty of the Kingdom of Dublin took over.
kingdom-of-york.r: Jorvik grew into a major town of craftsmen and traders, with goods from Scandinavia to the Middle East, as the Coppergate excavations show. Its kings minted coins, some with Christian symbols, and cooperated with the archbishops of York. Scandinavian settlement left hundreds of place-names across Yorkshire.
kingdom-of-york.e: Aethelstan seized York in 927, but Norse kings such as Olaf Guthfrithson, Amlaib Cuaran and Eric Bloodaxe returned repeatedly. Eric's expulsion and death in 954 ended the kingdom, and York became part of the Kingdom of England as an earldom.

kingdom-of-the-hwicce.t: An Anglo-Saxon sub-kingdom of the lower Severn valley around Worcester, ruled by its own kings under Mercian overlordship.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.o: The Hwicce took shape in Gloucestershire, Worcestershire and western Warwickshire after the West Saxon victory at Dyrham in 577 opened the region to English settlement. By the 7th century the area was ruled by a local dynasty, possibly installed or confirmed by Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.r: Hwiccan kings such as Osric and Oshere founded minsters including Bath, Gloucester and Pershore, and a bishopric was created at Worcester around 680 to serve the people. The territory was rich in salt from Droitwich and in farmland, and its charters are among the earliest English documents.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.e: Hwiccan rulers were downgraded from kings to ealdormen in the late 8th century under Offa. The kingdom's boundaries survived as the medieval diocese of Worcester, preserving its outline for centuries.

kingdom-of-corsica.t: The eight-month kingdom of Theodore von Neuhoff, a German adventurer crowned by Corsican rebels against Genoa in 1736.
kingdom-of-corsica.o: Corsicans had been in revolt against Genoese rule since 1729. In March 1736 Theodore von Neuhoff, a Westphalian baron, landed with arms and money from Tunis, and in April the rebel leaders crowned him king at the convent of Alesani, with a constitution limiting his power.
kingdom-of-corsica.r: Theodore set up a court at Cervione, created orders of knighthood, minted coins and issued titles, but failed to take the Genoese-held coastal towns. Promised foreign aid did not arrive, and his support among the rebel chiefs waned.
kingdom-of-corsica.e: In November 1736 Theodore left Corsica to seek help. His later attempts to return failed, and he ended in a London debtors' prison, dying in 1756. The revolt continued and later produced the Corsican Republic.

kingdom-of-marion.t: Cypriot kingdom on the north-west coast that grew rich on copper trade with Athens until Ptolemy I destroyed it in 312 BCE.
kingdom-of-marion.o: Marion grew near modern Polis Chrysochous in north-west Cyprus, close to the copper mines of Limni, in the early Iron Age. It emerged as a city-kingdom in the Cypro-Archaic period, facing Anatolia and the Aegean across the sea.
kingdom-of-marion.r: Marion exported copper and imported large quantities of Athenian painted pottery, found in its cemeteries. Its kings, some with Greek names such as Stasioikos and others possibly Phoenician, issued coins in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. Inscriptions use the Cypriot syllabary for Greek.
kingdom-of-marion.e: Its last king, Stasioikos II, sided with Antigonus against Ptolemy I, who destroyed Marion in 312 BCE and moved its people to Paphos. Ptolemy II refounded the site as Arsinoe c. 270 BCE, and the modern town of Polis stands there today.

kingdom-of-pengwern.t: A shadowy British kingdom of the Shropshire borderlands, remembered in the Welsh poems lamenting Cynddylan and the ruin of his hall.
kingdom-of-pengwern.o: Pengwern is known almost entirely from Welsh poetry, notably the Canu Heledd, a 9th or 10th century cycle of poems lamenting Cynddylan, a 7th century prince. Its centre is uncertain; later tradition placed it at Shrewsbury, while scholars suggest the Wrekin area or Din Gwrygon.
kingdom-of-pengwern.r: Nothing reliable is recorded of its government. The poems describe Cynddylan's hall at Eglwysau Bassa and his wars against the English, and he may have been an ally of Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia. The kingdom was probably one of several successors to the Cornovii tribal region.
kingdom-of-pengwern.e: Pengwern seems to have fallen to Mercian expansion in the mid 7th century; Cynddylan's death is lamented in the poems. Its lands became Mercian, while its memory survived in Welsh literature as a symbol of loss.

kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.t: Early Welsh kingdom of the Tywi valley in Carmarthenshire, conquered around 730 by Ceredigion to form the realm of Seisyllwg.
kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.o: Ystrad Tywi, 'the vale of the Tywi', covered the fertile river valley and surrounding uplands of what is now Carmarthenshire, including the old Roman town of Moridunum, Carmarthen. After Roman rule ended around 410 it seems to have emerged as a separate territory, sometimes held by the kings of the neighbouring Kingdom of Dyfed.
kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.r: Very little is known about its rulers or government, and no secure king list survives. The Tywi valley was among the best farmland in south-west Wales, with major church sites such as Llandeilo Fawr, home of the gospel book now known as the Lichfield Gospels before it left Wales.
kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.e: Around 730 Seisyll ap Clydog of the Kingdom of Ceredigion conquered Ystrad Tywi, forming a larger kingdom named Seisyllwg after him. This passed in the 10th century to Hywel Dda and became part of Deheubarth, whose later princes ruled from Dinefwr in the Tywi valley.

kingdom-of-gwent.t: Welsh kingdom between the Usk and the Wye, heir to the Roman town of Caerwent, which fell to the Normans after 1067.
kingdom-of-gwent.o: Gwent took its name from Venta Silurum, Caerwent, the Roman capital of the Silures. After Roman rule ended a kingdom formed in the land between the Usk and the Wye, with traditions of a founder named Caradog Freichfras. Its kings were often the same as those of the Kingdom of Glywysing, the two realms passing between branches of one dynasty.
kingdom-of-gwent.r: The Llandaff charters record grants by its kings to churches and show a landscape of royal estates and small monasteries. Brochfael ap Meurig submitted to Alfred of Wessex, according to Asser. The kingdom lay on the English border, and its rulers alternately fought and allied with the Mercians and later the English kings, while the fertile Usk valley and coastal levels provided its wealth.
kingdom-of-gwent.e: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn seized Gwent in the 1050s. After the Norman Conquest William FitzOsbern built Chepstow Castle from 1067 and pushed west. Its last king, Caradog ap Gruffudd, was killed at the battle of Mynydd Carn in 1081, and Gwent became Norman marcher lordships, later Monmouthshire.

kingdom-of-orleans.t: Short-lived Merovingian kingdom of Clovis' son Chlodomer, which vanished when he fell in battle in 524.
kingdom-of-orleans.o: In the division of 511 Clovis' second son Chlodomer received lands along the Loire, with Orléans as his capital, together with Tours, Bourges and part of Aquitaine.
kingdom-of-orleans.r: Chlodomer ruled for only thirteen years. Little is known of his government beyond his wars against the Kingdom of the Burgundians, during which he had the captured King Sigismund and his family killed in 524.
kingdom-of-orleans.e: Chlodomer was killed later in 524 at the Battle of Vézeronce. His uncles Childebert I and Chlothar I murdered two of his young sons and divided his kingdom. The third son, Clodoald, escaped and became a monk; the town of Saint-Cloud near Paris is named after him.

kingdom-of-murcia.t: A Castilian frontier kingdom in south-eastern Spain, formed after the reconquest of Murcia and kept as a historical unit until 1833.
kingdom-of-murcia.o: After the Mudéjar revolt of 1264-1266, James I of Aragon conquered Murcia on behalf of his son-in-law Alfonso X of Castile, ending the Third Taifa of Murcia. Alfonso X resettled the territory with Castilians and Catalans and kept it as a separate kingdom within the Crown of Castile.
kingdom-of-murcia.r: Murcia was a frontier facing both the Emirate of Granada and the Crown of Aragon, which took its northern districts by the Treaty of Torrellas in 1304. The irrigated huertas produced silk, fruit and grain, the Mudéjar population declined, and Cartagena grew into the main naval base on the Mediterranean.
kingdom-of-murcia.e: The kingdom was a historical title and administrative unit rather than a self-governing state. In 1833 Javier de Burgos's reform divided Spain into provinces, splitting the old kingdom into the provinces of Murcia and Albacete.

kingdom-of-tethba.t: A midland Irish kingdom spanning Longford and Westmeath, held by branches of the southern Ui Neill and later by the O'Farrells and O'Quinns.
kingdom-of-tethba.o: Tethba appears in the earliest Irish annals as a territory in the Irish midlands, divided by the River Inny into northern and southern parts. Its rulers in the early medieval period came from Cairpre and Maine, sons of Niall of the Nine Hostages, making it part of the southern Ui Neill world centred on Mide.
kingdom-of-tethba.r: Tethba was a small overkingship of several local peoples, often subordinate to the kings of Mide. Monasteries such as Ardagh and Clonmacnoise's daughter houses stood in or near its lands. In the 11th and 12th centuries local families, the Ui Cuinn and the Ui Fergail, rose to power in the northern part, later known as Annaly.
kingdom-of-tethba.e: After the Norman invasion much of southern Tethba was granted to Hugh de Lacy within the Lordship of Meath. Annaly survived under the O'Farrells until the 16th century, when it became County Longford.

kingdom-of-rhufoniog.t: Small early Welsh kingdom between the Conwy and Clwyd valleys, named in legend after a son of Cunedda, later a cantref of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-rhufoniog.o: Welsh tradition, preserved in genealogies written down centuries later, says the district took its name from Rhufon, one of the sons of Cunedda who came from the north to settle north Wales in the 5th century. The story is a later origin legend, but Rhufoniog existed as a distinct territory in the uplands of what is now Denbighshire.
kingdom-of-rhufoniog.r: Very little is known of its rulers or government. It was one of several small early kingdoms of north Wales whose local dynasties appear in medieval genealogies, and its territory included the hills around Denbigh. Farming and cattle-rearing were the mainstay of a thinly settled land.
kingdom-of-rhufoniog.e: By the 9th century Rhufoniog had been absorbed into the Kingdom of Gwynedd and later formed one of the cantrefi of the Perfeddwlad, the borderland between Gwynedd and England contested by Welsh princes and English kings until 1283.

kingdom-of-portugal.t: One of Europe's oldest kingdoms, which fixed its borders by 1249, led the age of oceanic exploration and lasted until the revolution of 1910.
kingdom-of-portugal.o: The County of Portugal, a fief of León, passed to Afonso Henriques, who styled himself king after his victory at Ourique in 1139. León recognised him at Zamora in 1143 and the papacy in 1179. With crusader help he took Lisbon in 1147, and Afonso III completed the conquest of the Algarve in 1249.
kingdom-of-portugal.r: Portugal was a Catholic monarchy with Cortes, military orders and a strong maritime economy. After the victory of Aljubarrota in 1385, John I founded the Aviz dynasty, whose princes launched the voyages that created the Portuguese Empire. Pepper, Brazilian sugar and gold financed the crown. Manuel I ruled at the peak of the spice trade.
kingdom-of-portugal.e: The kingdom fell under Spanish kings in the Iberian Union from 1580 to 1640, then revived under the Braganzas. After the 1908 assassination of Carlos I, a revolution on 5 October 1910 ended the monarchy and created the First Portuguese Republic.

kingdom-of-noricum.t: A Celtic kingdom in the eastern Alps, famed for its iron and steel, that became a Roman ally and then a Roman province without a major war.
kingdom-of-noricum.o: Noricum grew out of a union of Celtic tribes in the eastern Alps, led by the Norici, during the 2nd century BCE. Its core lay in modern Carinthia and Styria, around the Magdalensberg and a centre the Romans called Noreia. In 113 BCE Rome defended it against the migrating Cimbri, who defeated a Roman army at Noreia.
kingdom-of-noricum.r: The kingdom was ruled by kings over a federation of tribes and was known across the Mediterranean for ferrum Noricum, a high-quality steel produced from local ores. Italian merchants settled at the Magdalensberg trading post, and Noricum minted its own silver coins. Close ties with Rome made it a client kingdom; its king Voccio sent cavalry to Julius Caesar in 49 BCE.
kingdom-of-noricum.e: Around 16 BCE Noricum was absorbed peacefully into the Roman Empire, becoming the province of Noricum with towns such as Virunum and Celeia. Roman rule lasted until the late 5th century, when the Life of Saint Severinus records the last Roman communities before their evacuation in 488.

knidos.t: Dorian port city on a Carian peninsula, home of Praxiteles's Aphrodite, the astronomer Eudoxus and a renowned school of medicine.
knidos.o: Dorian Greeks settled Knidos at the tip of a long peninsula in south-west Anatolia in the early first millennium BCE. It belonged to the Dorian Hexapolis with Kos, Halicarnassus and the three Rhodian cities of Lindos, Ialysos and Kamiros, which met at the sanctuary of Apollo at Triopion in Knidian territory.
knidos.r: Knidos was an oligarchy run by a council of sixty, and grew rich on trade, wine and its double harbour. When the Persian general Harpagus advanced c. 545 BCE, the Knidians tried to cut through their isthmus but submitted. The city later produced the astronomer Eudoxus, the physician Ctesias and Sostratus, architect of the Pharos of Alexandria; its treasury and clubhouse stood at Delphi.
knidos.e: Off Knidos in 394 BCE Conon's Persian-backed fleet destroyed Spartan sea power. In the 4th century BCE the city moved to the cape, where Praxiteles's nude Aphrodite drew visitors. It joined the Roman province of Asia in 129 BCE as a free city.

kingdom-of-ailech.t: Kingdom of the northern Uí Néill based at the stone fort of Grianan of Aileach, whose Cenél nEógain kings often held the high kingship of Ireland.
kingdom-of-ailech.o: Ailech emerged in the early medieval period as the kingdom of the northern Uí Néill, descendants of Niall of the Nine Hostages who expanded into the north-west in the 5th and 6th centuries. It took its name from the hilltop stone fort of Grianan of Aileach on the Inishowen peninsula, which served as a royal centre.
kingdom-of-ailech.r: The kingdom was dominated by the Cenél nEógain, who displaced the Cenél Conaill from the kingship in the 8th century and alternated the high kingship with the southern Uí Néill. Kings such as Áed Findliath and Niall Glúndub, killed fighting the Vikings of Dublin in 919, were among the most powerful in Ireland. The Mac Lochlainn line, notably Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn, held the high kingship in the 12th century.
kingdom-of-ailech.e: In 1101 Muirchertach Ua Briain of Munster demolished Grianan of Aileach in revenge for an earlier attack on Kincora. Power within Cenél nEógain passed from the Mac Lochlainns to the Ua Néill, and the kingdom of Ailech became the O'Neill kingdom of Tír Eógain, Tyrone.

kingdom-of-cambrai.t: Small Frankish kingdom around Cambrai, ruled by Clovis' kinsman Ragnachar until Clovis eliminated him.
kingdom-of-cambrai.o: Cambrai was taken by the Salian king Chlodio in the mid 5th century, and by the 480s it was the seat of a separate Frankish king, Ragnachar, a relative of Clovis. Known almost only from Gregory of Tours.
kingdom-of-cambrai.r: Ragnachar joined Clovis against Syagrius and the Domain of Soissons in 486. Gregory portrays him as a debauched ruler who lost the loyalty of his warriors.
kingdom-of-cambrai.e: Around 509 Clovis bribed Ragnachar's followers with armlets of gilded bronze passed off as gold, defeated him and killed him and his brother Richar with his own axe. Cambrai was absorbed into the Kingdom of the Franks.

kingdom-of-waterford.t: A Norse town-kingdom at the mouth of the Suir, the oldest city in Ireland, until its storming by the Anglo-Normans in 1170.
kingdom-of-waterford.o: Vikings raided the south-east in the 9th century, and in 914 a large fleet under Ragnall established a base at Waterford, Vedrafjordr. The settlement grew into a fortified trading town ruled by Norse kings or jarls, sometimes linked to the Kingdom of Dublin.
kingdom-of-waterford.r: Waterford traded wine, slaves and goods across the Irish Sea and to France. Its rulers became Christian and accepted bishops consecrated at Canterbury from 1096. Irish overkings of Munster, especially the O'Briens, often controlled the town, and Reginald's Tower recalls its Norse defences.
kingdom-of-waterford.e: In 1170 Strongbow and Raymond le Gros stormed the town, and Strongbow married Aoife, daughter of Diarmait Mac Murchada, there. Henry II landed at Waterford in 1171 and made it a royal city in the Lordship of Ireland.

kingdom-of-connacht.t: Western Irish province-kingdom whose O'Connor kings, Toirdelbach and Ruaidrí, became high kings before Anglo-Norman conquest reduced it.
kingdom-of-connacht.o: The Connachta, who gave the province its name, claimed descent from Conn of the Hundred Battles. By the 6th century their branches, the Uí Briúin and Uí Fiachrach, ruled the west, with kings inaugurated at Cruachan, the great ritual site of Rathcroghan in Roscommon. The Uí Briúin gradually took control of the over-kingship.
kingdom-of-connacht.r: Kings ruled through a network of subject kingdoms such as the Kingdom of Ui Maine. The Ua Conchobair, O'Connor, line rose in the 11th century; Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair, king from 1106 to 1156, built bridges and castles, divided Munster and claimed the high kingship. His son Ruaidrí became the last High King of Ireland and agreed the Treaty of Windsor with Henry II in 1175.
kingdom-of-connacht.e: Anglo-Norman lords led by the de Burghs received a grant of Connacht in 1227, and the O'Connors were confined to Roscommon. Splits between rival O'Connor branches in the 14th century weakened the kingship further, and the title faded out in the later 15th century.
kingdom-of-connacht.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-iarmumu.t: The early medieval kingdom of West Munster around Killarney's lakes, ruled by the Eoganacht Locha Lein, rivals of the Munster kings at Cashel.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.o: Iarmumu took shape in south-west Ireland by the 6th century, when the Eoganacht Locha Lein, a branch of the dynasties ruling Munster, established themselves around Loch Lein, the Lower Lake at Killarney. Their territory covered much of later Kerry and west Cork, absorbing earlier peoples such as the Corcu Duibne.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.r: The kings of Iarmumu sometimes claimed the kingship of all Munster, but were usually excluded from the rotation of Cashel's Eoganacht branches. Inisfallen on Loch Lein became an important monastery, later home of the Annals of Inisfallen. Cattle wealth and client peoples supported the dynasty.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.e: By the 8th and 9th centuries the dynasty weakened, and other lineages gained ground in Kerry, notably the Ui Donnchada. In the 12th century the area fell within the Kingdom of Desmond under the MacCarthys, with the O'Donoghues as local lords around Killarney.

kingdom-of-great-britain.t: The kingdom created by the union of England and Scotland in 1707, which became Europe's leading maritime and commercial power in the 18th century.
kingdom-of-great-britain.o: The Acts of Union of 1707, passed by the Kingdom of England and the Kingdom of Scotland, merged them into one kingdom with a single Parliament at Westminster, while Scotland kept its own law, church and education. The two countries had shared a monarch since 1603.
kingdom-of-great-britain.r: Great Britain developed cabinet government under Robert Walpole and the Hanoverian kings from 1714. It defeated Jacobite risings in 1715 and 1745. Trade, the Bank of England and naval power built an empire in North America, the Caribbean and India, and the Seven Years' War brought Canada. The American colonies were lost in 1783, while the Industrial Revolution began.
kingdom-of-great-britain.e: The Acts of Union of 1800 joined Great Britain with the Kingdom of Ireland to form the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland on 1 January 1801.
kingdom-of-great-britain.re: Christianity; Church of England, Church of Scotland

kingdom-of-meirionnydd.t: Early Welsh kingdom between the Mawddach and the Dyfi, named after a grandson of Cunedda, which gave its name to the later county of Merioneth.
kingdom-of-meirionnydd.o: According to Welsh genealogical tradition, Meirionnydd took its name from Meirion, a grandson of Cunedda, who was granted the land between the rivers Mawddach and Dyfi in the 5th century. Like other Cunedda stories, this is a later legend, but a separate royal line for Meirionnydd is recorded in medieval genealogies.
kingdom-of-meirionnydd.r: Little is recorded of its government. The kingdom covered a mountainous coastal region including Cadair Idris, with farming on the valley floors and the coast, and its people were linked by sea with the rest of Cardigan Bay. Its kings appear to have been subordinate to the more powerful rulers of the Kingdom of Gwynedd for much of their history.
kingdom-of-meirionnydd.e: Meirionnydd was absorbed into the Kingdom of Gwynedd, probably by the 10th century, becoming one of its cantrefi. After the English conquest of 1283 it formed the core of the county of Merioneth, and the name survives in the region of Meirionnydd today.

kingdom-of-buellt.t: Small Welsh kingdom around Builth Wells, ruled by a dynasty claiming descent from Vortigern, and later the place where Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was killed.
kingdom-of-buellt.o: Buellt lay in the middle Wye and Irfon valleys around modern Builth Wells. The Historia Brittonum of about 829 says Ambrosius granted Buellt and Gwrtheyrnion to Pascent, son of Vortigern, and names Fernmail as the ruler of both in the author's own day. Among its wonders it lists Carn Cabal, a cairn said to bear the footprint of Arthur's hound.
kingdom-of-buellt.r: Little is recorded of its government. It was a small upland kingdom of river valleys and hill grazing, generally ruled together with the Kingdom of Gwrtheyrnion and lying between the larger realms of the Kingdom of Powys, the Kingdom of Brycheiniog and the south-western kingdoms.
kingdom-of-buellt.e: Buellt was absorbed by larger Welsh kingdoms in the 10th century and later became a cantref contested between Welsh princes and Norman lords, with a castle at Builth. In 1282 Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, last native Prince of Wales, was killed near Cilmeri in Buellt.

karystos.t: City of southern Euboea, forced into the Delian League by Athens and later famed for its green-veined Cipollino marble.
karystos.o: Karystos lay at the southern end of Euboea, below Mount Ochi. Greek tradition held that its people were Dryopes, later joined by Ionian settlers. It grew in the early Iron Age as a farming and seafaring community, controlling the channel between Euboea and Andros.
karystos.r: The Persians forced Karystos to submit in 490 BCE, and it fought on their side in 480 BCE. Athens then compelled it to join the Delian League c. 472 BCE. In the 4th century BCE it produced the physician Diocles, and later the writer Antigonus. Its green-veined marble, Cipollino, was quarried heavily in Roman times.
karystos.e: Karystos passed between Macedonian kings and Athens in the Hellenistic period and came under Roman control by 146 BCE. Its marble quarries remained important under the Empire, and the modern town keeps the ancient name.

kingdom-of-the-gepids.t: East Germanic kingdom in the Tisza plain and Transylvania that rose after Attila's empire collapsed and was destroyed by Lombards and Avars in 567.
kingdom-of-the-gepids.o: The Gepids, a Gothic-related people, were subjects of Attila's Huns. In 454 their king Ardaric led the revolt that crushed Attila's sons at the River Nedao, and the Gepids took over the lands east of the Danube in the Tisza plain and Transylvania.
kingdom-of-the-gepids.r: Gepid kings ruled a mixed population of Germanic, Sarmatian and local peoples, and adopted Arian Christianity. Rich princely graves such as those at Apahida show their wealth. They seized Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica) on the Sava, a key city, and competed with the Ostrogoths, Byzantium and the Lombards for the middle Danube. Kings Thurisind and Cunimund fought the Lombards in the 550s and 560s.
kingdom-of-the-gepids.e: In 567 the Lombards under Alboin, allied with the newly arrived Avars, destroyed the kingdom; Cunimund was killed and Alboin made his skull into a drinking cup. The Gepid lands passed to the Avar Khaganate.

kingdom-of-essex.t: The kingdom of the East Saxons north of the Thames, which controlled London for long periods and had a dynasty with unusual 'S' names.
kingdom-of-essex.o: The East Saxons settled Essex, Middlesex and parts of Hertfordshire. Their royal genealogy traces kings to Aescwine, traditionally placed in 527, and later kings bore names beginning with S, such as Saeberht, Sigeberht and Swithred.
kingdom-of-essex.r: Essex held London, which Bede called a market of many peoples. Saeberht accepted Christianity around 604 and Mellitus became bishop of London, but the kingdom reverted to paganism after his death until Cedd's mission in the 650s. Several kings often ruled jointly. Essex usually stood under the overlordship of Kent or Mercia.
kingdom-of-essex.e: After 825 Essex submitted to Ecgberht of the Kingdom of Wessex, and later fell within the Danelaw. In the 10th century it was absorbed into the Kingdom of England as a shire, which survives as the county of Essex.

kingdom-of-the-swedes.t: Early kingdom of the Svear around Lake Mälaren and Uppsala, whose kings ruled the trading town of Birka and later united the Swedish lands.
kingdom-of-the-swedes.o: Tacitus wrote of the Suiones in the 1st century, and by the 6th century the Svear had a power centre at Old Uppsala, where great royal mounds were raised. Rich boat graves at Vendel and Valsgärde show a wealthy warrior elite. Later sagas trace the kings to the legendary Yngling dynasty.
kingdom-of-the-swedes.r: Kingship was tied to the pagan cult at Uppsala, described by Adam of Bremen, and to assemblies of free men at the thing. Birka, founded in the 8th century on Lake Mälaren, linked the kingdom to trade routes east to Rus' and the Byzantine and Abbasid worlds. Rimbert's life of Ansgar records kings Björn and Anund receiving the Frankish missionary around 830 and 850.
kingdom-of-the-swedes.e: Eric the Victorious, who defeated a rival at Fýrisvellir in the 980s, and his son Olof Skötkonung extended Svear rule over the Geats. This union of the Svear and Götar is regarded as the start of the medieval Kingdom of Sweden, and the Uppsala kingship gave Sweden its name.

kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.t: A tiny Jutish kingdom on the Isle of Wight, the last part of England to accept Christianity, ended by the violent conquest of Caedwalla in 686.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.o: Bede reports that the Isle of Wight, like Kent and part of Hampshire, was settled by Jutes. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle claims that Cerdic and Cynric took the island in 530 and gave it to their kinsmen Stuf and Wihtgar, but the story is largely legendary.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.r: The Wihtwara lived from farming and the sea under their own kings, sometimes dependents of greater neighbours. In 661 Wulfhere of the Kingdom of Mercia gave the island to the South Saxon king Aethelwealh. The island was still pagan in the 680s.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.e: In 686 Caedwalla of the Kingdom of Wessex conquered the island, killed King Arwald and had his two young brothers executed after baptism, as Bede recounts. The island became part of Wessex and was converted by Wilfrid's clergy.

kingdom-of-greece.t: The Greek monarchy from 1832 to 1973, which more than doubled Greece's territory and lived through the National Schism, occupation, civil war and dictatorship.
kingdom-of-greece.o: Under the London Conference of 1832, Britain, France and Russia made Otto of Bavaria king of independent Greece, replacing the First Hellenic Republic. He arrived at Nauplia in 1833 with Bavarian regents, and Athens became the capital in 1834. A revolt in September 1843 forced him to grant a constitution.
kingdom-of-greece.r: Otto was deposed in 1862 and replaced by George I, whose long reign added the Ionian Islands (1864), Thessaly (1881) and, through the Balkan Wars, Macedonia, Epirus and Crete. Politics were shaped by the Great Idea of uniting Greeks and by the clash between Eleftherios Venizelos and King Constantine I. Defeat in Asia Minor in 1922 brought a population exchange with Turkey.
kingdom-of-greece.e: The monarchy was replaced by the Second Hellenic Republic in 1924 and restored in 1935, followed by the Metaxas dictatorship, Axis occupation and civil war. After the 1967 coup, Constantine II went into exile; the junta abolished the monarchy in 1973, confirmed by referendum in 1974.

keos.t: Cycladic island state of four small cities nearest to Attica, home of the poets Simonides and Bacchylides.
keos.o: Keos lies off the tip of Attica and had a major Bronze Age town at Ayia Irini. In the early Iron Age Ionian Greeks settled it, and the island was organised as a tetrapolis of four cities, Ioulis, Karthaia, Koressia and Poiessa, which sometimes acted together as one state.
keos.r: Keos was famous for its poets: Simonides and his nephew Bacchylides, both from Ioulis, wrote for patrons across Greece in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE. Strabo records a Keian law said to require citizens over sixty to drink hemlock. The island exported ruddle, a red earth pigment, and paid tribute in the Delian League.
keos.e: Keos joined the Second Athenian League but revolted in the 360s BCE and was subdued. In the 3rd century BCE Koressia became a Ptolemaic naval base renamed Arsinoe. The island passed under Roman control by 146 BCE.

kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.t: The short-lived sea realm of Somerled, who seized the southern Hebrides from the kings of Man and founded the dynasty of the Lords of the Isles.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.o: Somerled, a Norse-Gaelic warlord of Argyll married to a daughter of Olaf I of Man, challenged his brother-in-law Godred of the Kingdom of the Isles. After a sea battle in 1156 the Hebrides were divided, and in 1158 Somerled drove Godred from Man, ruling Argyll, Kintyre and the southern isles.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.r: Somerled's power rested on galley fleets and the loyalty of Gaelic and Norse-Gaelic kindreds. He acted as an independent ruler, sometimes allied with and sometimes against the Scottish king, and is linked with the founding of Saddell Abbey in Kintyre.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.e: Somerled was killed in 1164 at Renfrew while invading the Kingdom of Scotland. His realm was divided among his sons, ancestors of the MacDougalls, MacDonalds and MacRuairis, whose descendants later formed the Lordship of the Isles.

kingdom-of-italy-medieval.t: The medieval Kingdom of Italy, contested by Italian magnates after 888 and then held by the German emperors, whose authority waned as the cities grew.
kingdom-of-italy-medieval.o: When the Carolingian Empire broke up in 888, Italian nobles elected Berengar of Friuli as King of Italy. For seventy years rival magnates and outsiders, among them Guy and Lambert of Spoleto, Louis of Provence, Rudolf of Burgundy and Hugh of Arles, fought for the crown, which was traditionally received at Pavia.
kingdom-of-italy-medieval.r: In 951 Otto I of Germany took the title, and from his imperial coronation in 962 the crown was tied to the German emperors, often crowned with the Iron Crown of Lombardy. Arduin of Ivrea was the last native king (1002–1014). Imperial rule relied on bishops and counts, but the communes grew independent; the Lombard League defeated Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176, and the Peace of Constance in 1183 recognised their self-government.
kingdom-of-italy-medieval.e: After the 13th century the kingdom survived mainly as a legal framework of imperial fiefs. Charles V was the last emperor crowned King of Italy, at Bologna in 1530. Imperial claims in Italy ended with the French Revolutionary Wars and the Treaty of Lunéville in 1801.

kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.t: Tiny Welsh kingdom between the Wye and the Ithon whose rulers claimed descent from Vortigern, the British ruler blamed for inviting the Saxons.
kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.o: Gwrtheyrnion means 'the land of Gwrtheyrn', the Welsh form of Vortigern. The Historia Brittonum, written in 829 or 830, says that after Vortigern's fall his son Pascent was granted Buellt and Gwrtheyrnion by Ambrosius, and that its ruler in the author's day, Fernmail, descended from him. The territory lay around Rhayader in what became Radnorshire.
kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.r: Almost nothing is known of its government beyond this genealogy. It was a small upland territory of river valleys and hill pasture, often ruled together with the neighbouring Kingdom of Buellt, and its dynasty used its link with Vortigern, whatever its truth, to assert ancient legitimacy.
kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.e: Gwrtheyrnion was absorbed by more powerful Welsh kingdoms, probably in the 10th century, and later formed a cantref of the Middle March between Wye and Severn, held by Welsh and Anglo-Norman lords such as the Mortimers.

kingdom-of-gododdin.t: British kingdom of Lothian centred on Edinburgh, celebrated in the early Welsh poem Y Gododdin, which fell to Northumbria in the 7th century.
kingdom-of-gododdin.o: Gododdin was the post-Roman kingdom of the Votadini, whose name became Guotodin and then Gododdin in Welsh. Its centre was Din Eidyn, the rock of Edinburgh, and it stretched across Lothian and the eastern Borders. Welsh tradition also linked the district of Manaw Gododdin, around the head of the Forth, with Cunedda, legendary founder of the Kingdom of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-gododdin.r: The kingdom is best known from Y Gododdin, attributed to the poet Aneirin, which mourns a war band feasted for a year by Mynyddog Mwynfawr at Din Eidyn and then slaughtered at Catraeth, usually identified as Catterick, around 600. The poem portrays an aristocratic warrior society bound by loyalty, mead and gifts. Hillforts such as Traprain Law and Edinburgh Castle Rock were key centres.
kingdom-of-gododdin.e: The Anglian kingdom of Bernicia, later Northumbria, expanded northward in the 7th century. Irish annals record the siege of Etin in 638, generally taken as the Northumbrian capture of Edinburgh. Lothian remained English until it passed to the Scottish kings in the 10th and 11th centuries.

kingdom-of-germany.t: The German kingdom at the heart of the Holy Roman Empire, an elective monarchy whose kings claimed the imperial crown for more than eight centuries.
kingdom-of-germany.o: The kingdom grew out of East Francia. Its kings, from Henry the Fowler in 919, were elected by the great nobles. When Otto I was crowned emperor in Rome in 962, the German crown became joined with the imperial title and with kingship of Italy and later Burgundy, a link that defined the Holy Roman Empire.
kingdom-of-germany.r: German kings were elected, from 1356 by the seven prince-electors under the Golden Bull, and crowned at Aachen. Royal power weakened during the Investiture Controversy and after the fall of the Hohenstaufen, while princes, bishops and free cities gained autonomy. From 1438 the Habsburgs held the crown almost without break, governing with the Imperial Diet.
kingdom-of-germany.e: The Reformation and the Thirty Years' War, ended by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, left Germany a federation of nearly sovereign states. Under Napoleonic pressure, Francis II abdicated on 6 August 1806, dissolving the Empire and the German kingdom with it.
kingdom-of-germany.re: Catholic Christianity, Lutheranism and Calvinism after 1517

kingdom-of-ulaid.t: The ancient over-kingdom of Ulster, linked in legend with Emain Macha and the Ulster Cycle, which shrank to Antrim and Down before the Anglo-Normans.
kingdom-of-ulaid.o: The Ulaid, probably Ptolemy's Voluntii, gave their name to Ulster. Irish tradition remembers them as rulers of the whole north from Emain Macha, Navan Fort near Armagh, the setting of the Ulster Cycle tales of Conchobar mac Nessa and Cú Chulainn. In the 5th century, according to tradition, the Three Collas and the Uí Néill drove them east of the River Bann.
kingdom-of-ulaid.r: In historic times the kingdom was an over-kingship shared between the Dal Fiatach of Down and the Dal nAraidi of Antrim. Kings such as Báetán mac Cairill and Congal Cáech challenged the Uí Néill, but defeat at Mag Rath in 637 ended their hopes of wider supremacy. The kingdom's monasteries, including Bangor, Movilla and Nendrum, were among the great centres of early Irish learning.
kingdom-of-ulaid.e: Viking raids and Uí Néill pressure confined the Ulaid to Antrim and Down. In 1177 John de Courcy captured Downpatrick and defeated Ruaidrí Mac Duinn Sléibe, and the Ulaid lands became the Anglo-Norman Earldom of Ulster.

kingdom-of-mercia.t: The great midland kingdom that dominated England in the 8th century under Aethelbald and Offa, whose Dyke still marks the Welsh border.
kingdom-of-mercia.o: Mercia, the 'border people', arose among Angles in the upper Trent valley. Later genealogies place its first kings, Icel and Creoda, in the 6th century, but the first well-attested ruler is the pagan Penda, who fought Northumbria and East Anglia from the 620s to his death at the Winwaed in 655.
kingdom-of-mercia.r: Mercian kings ruled from Tamworth, with a bishopric at Lichfield, and dominated client kingdoms such as the Hwicce and the Magonsaete. Offa took the title king of the English, issued a reformed silver penny, corresponded with Charlemagne and built Offa's Dyke. He briefly created an archbishopric at Lichfield.
kingdom-of-mercia.e: Defeat by Wessex at Ellendun in 825 and the Viking conquests of the 870s split Mercia. Its western half, under Aethelred and Aethelflaed, the Lady of the Mercians, allied with Wessex. After Aethelflaed's death in 918 it was absorbed into the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons.

kingdom-of-lindsey.t: A small Anglian kingdom in north Lincolnshire centred on Roman Lincoln, briefly fought over by Northumbria and Mercia before Mercian absorption.
kingdom-of-lindsey.o: Lindsey took its name from the Roman Lindum (Lincoln), and Anglian settlers established a kingdom there in the late 5th or 6th century. A list of its kings survives in a collection of royal genealogies, tracing them to Woden, ending with Aldfrith in the late 8th century.
kingdom-of-lindsey.r: The kingdom lay between the Humber and the Witham, bounded by fen and sea, and was too small to stand alone. Paulinus preached at Lincoln around 628 under Northumbrian protection, building a stone church. A separate bishopric of Lindsey was founded in 678.
kingdom-of-lindsey.e: Northumbria and Mercia contested Lindsey until the Battle of the Trent in 679 left it permanently Mercian. Its kings faded into dependent rulers and disappeared by about 800. The district was later settled by Danes and formed part of Lincolnshire.

kingdom-of-paeonia.t: Ancient kingdom of the Axios (Vardar) valley north of Macedon, whose kings minted fine silver coins before falling under Macedonian control.
kingdom-of-paeonia.o: The Paeonians held the Axios and Strymon valleys from early times; Homer lists them as allies of Troy. In 511 BCE the Persian general Megabazus deported many of them to Asia. A kingdom with its own coinage emerged in the 4th century BCE, centred on Bylazora and Astibos (Štip).
kingdom-of-paeonia.r: Kings such as Lyppeios, Patraos and Audoleon issued silver coins showing Apollo and horsemen, and Audoleon was honoured at Athens. The economy rested on herding, farming and the trade route along the Axios. The Paeonians worshipped the sun and a Dionysus called Dyalos, and were famed riders. Philip II of Macedon forced them into dependency after 358 BCE, and they served in Alexander's army.
kingdom-of-paeonia.e: Celtic invasions in 279 BCE weakened the kingdom. In 217 BCE Philip V of Macedon took Bylazora, ending its independence, and after 168 BCE Paeonia became part of Roman Macedonia.

kingdom-of-pergamon.t: Hellenistic kingdom of the Attalid dynasty in western Anatolia, a great centre of art and learning that was bequeathed to Rome in 133 BCE.
kingdom-of-pergamon.o: Philetaerus, an officer guarding Lysimachus' treasure of 9,000 talents at the citadel of Pergamon, changed sides to Seleucus I in 282 BCE and kept the fortress and money. His nephew Eumenes I asserted independence from the Seleucids. Attalus I took the title of king around 238 BCE after defeating the Galatians.
kingdom-of-pergamon.r: The Attalids built Pergamon into a showpiece capital of terraces, temples and theatre, with a library second only to Alexandria's, traditionally linked to the development of parchment. The Great Altar of Zeus celebrated victory over the Galatians. Loyal alliance with Rome brought Eumenes II wide lands in Asia Minor after the Peace of Apamea in 188 BCE.
kingdom-of-pergamon.e: Attalus III died in 133 BCE leaving his kingdom to Rome. Aristonicus, claiming to be a royal son, led a revolt that was crushed by 129 BCE, and the kingdom became the Roman province of Asia. The Pergamon Altar is now in Berlin.

kingdom-of-munster.t: Southern Irish over-kingdom ruled from the Rock of Cashel by the Eóganachta and later by the Dál Cais of Brian Bóruma, until it split in two in 1118.
kingdom-of-munster.o: Munster, Mumu in Irish, was one of the ancient provinces of Ireland. From around the 5th century the Eóganachta dynasties, tracing descent from Conall Corc, the legendary founder of Cashel, established an over-kingship over the province, displacing earlier Érainn peoples such as the Corcu Loigde.
kingdom-of-munster.r: Kings ruled from Cashel through a confederation of Eóganacht branches, collecting tribute from many subject peoples. Several were also churchmen or patrons of learning, such as Feidlimid mac Crimthainn, king and abbot, who died in 847. Cathal mac Finguine, who died in 742, challenged the Uí Néill for supremacy. In the 10th century the Dál Cais of Thomond took the kingship, and Brian Bóruma, king of Munster from 978, became High King of Ireland in 1002.
kingdom-of-munster.e: In 1101 Muirchertach Ua Briain gave the Rock of Cashel to the Church. In 1118 Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair of the Kingdom of Connacht divided Munster by the Treaty of Glanmire into Desmond, under the MacCarthys, and Thomond, under the O'Briens.

kingdom-of-sardinia.t: An island kingdom created for Aragon in the 14th century that passed to Savoy in 1720 and became the core of the Kingdom of Italy.
kingdom-of-sardinia.o: In 1297 Pope Boniface VIII created a Kingdom of Sardinia and Corsica for James II of the Kingdom of Aragon. His son Alfonso conquered the Pisan parts of the island in 1323–1324, founding the kingdom in fact.
kingdom-of-sardinia.r: Aragonese rule met long resistance from the Judicate of Arborea, whose Eleonora issued the Carta de Logu law code; Arborea fell in 1420. Sardinia was then governed by viceroys at Cagliari, under Aragon and Habsburg Spain, with its own parliament. Austria took it in 1708, and in 1720 the Treaty of The Hague gave it to Victor Amadeus II of the Duchy of Savoy, who ruled from Turin.
kingdom-of-sardinia.e: The Savoy kingdom joined Piedmont, Savoy and Nice; the Perfect Fusion of 1847 unified it, and Charles Albert granted the Statuto in 1848. Under Victor Emmanuel II and Cavour it led Italian unification, becoming the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

kingdom-of-etruria.t: A Napoleonic kingdom created in Tuscany for a Spanish Bourbon prince in 1801, abolished six years later.
kingdom-of-etruria.o: By agreements between France and Spain in 1800–1801, including the Treaty of Aranjuez, the Grand Duchy of Tuscany was taken from its Habsburg-Lorraine ruler and turned into the Kingdom of Etruria for Louis of Bourbon-Parma, in exchange for the Bourbon claim to the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza.
kingdom-of-etruria.r: Louis I, in poor health, ruled from Florence under strong French influence; the State of the Presidi was added. After his death in 1803 his widow Maria Luisa of Spain governed as regent for their young son Charles Louis. The court was conservative and pious, and the kingdom paid heavily to support French troops.
kingdom-of-etruria.e: In 1807 Napoleon dissolved the kingdom under the Treaty of Fontainebleau and annexed Tuscany to France in 1808. In 1809 he made his sister Elisa grand duchess. Maria Luisa later received the Duchy of Lucca.

kingdom-of-the-thuringians.t: A Germanic kingdom in central Germany, briefly one of the great powers of the post-Roman west until the Franks destroyed it in 531.
kingdom-of-the-thuringians.o: The Thuringians appear around 400 in a Roman veterinary text that praises their horses. They likely descended in part from the Hermunduri and Angles, and formed a kingdom centred on the Thuringian basin, extending at its height from the Harz to the Danube and from the Werra to the Elbe.
kingdom-of-the-thuringians.r: In the early 6th century King Herminafrid married Amalaberga, niece of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great, linking Thuringia to the Ostrogothic alliance system. Rich graves, horse burials and the trade in horses show an aristocratic warrior society. Little is known of its institutions, as it left no written records of its own.
kingdom-of-the-thuringians.e: After Theodoric's death removed Ostrogothic protection, the Frankish kings Theuderic I and Chlothar I defeated the Thuringians on the Unstrut in 531; Herminafrid was killed soon after at Zülpich. The north went to Saxon allies, the rest to the Franks, later forming the Duchy of Thuringia.

kingdom-of-galicia.t: The north-western Iberian kingdom centred on Santiago de Compostela, sometimes ruled by its own kings but usually joined with León and Castile.
kingdom-of-galicia.o: When Alfonso III of Asturias was deposed in 910, his son Ordoño II took Galicia as his kingdom. Galicia had been the core of the Kingdom of the Suebi and a part of the Asturian realm, and the cult of St James at Compostela had made it famous across Europe.
kingdom-of-galicia.r: Galicia was dominated by a powerful nobility and the church, above all the archbishops of Santiago such as Diego Gelmírez. It had its own kings at times, among them García II from 1065 to 1071, and Alfonso VII was crowned king of Galicia at Santiago in 1111. Galician-Portuguese became a major literary language, used for the troubadour lyric and the Cantigas de Santa Maria.
kingdom-of-galicia.e: From 1230 Galicia was permanently part of the Crown of Castile, though it kept the title of kingdom and from the 16th century its own Junta. The provincial reform of 1833 abolished it as an administrative unit, but Galicia today is an autonomous community.

kingdom-of-wessex.t: The kingdom of the West Saxons, which survived the Viking onslaught under Alfred the Great and grew into the Kingdom of England.
kingdom-of-wessex.o: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle traces Wessex to Cerdic and Cynric, said to have landed in 495 and taken the kingship in 519. Early kings of the Gewisse operated in the upper Thames valley before expanding west and south. Archaeology suggests more complex origins than the Chronicle's story.
kingdom-of-wessex.r: Wessex was divided into shires under ealdormen, with royal estates, law codes from Ine around 694, and bishoprics at Winchester and Sherborne. Christianity arrived with Birinus in 635. Victory over Mercia at Ellendun in 825 made Ecgberht the leading southern king. Alfred built a network of fortified burhs, a navy and a revival of learning in English.
kingdom-of-wessex.e: Alfred defeated Guthrum at Edington in 878 and his successors reconquered the Danelaw. From 886 Wessex merged into the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons, and under Aethelstan in 927 it became the core of the Kingdom of England, with Winchester its royal centre.

kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.t: The Gaelic lordship of north-west Ulster, ruled from the 13th century by the O'Donnells, whose flight in 1607 ended independent Gaelic rule in Ulster.
kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.o: Tir Chonaill, the land of Conall, was named after Conall Gulban, a son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. His descendants, the Cenel Conaill, formed one branch of the northern Ui Neill and held much of present-day County Donegal. Columba of Iona belonged to this kindred, which also shared the high kingship in the early centuries.
kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.r: Cenel Conaill kings alternated the northern overkingship with Cenel nEogain until the 8th century. From the 13th century the O'Donnell family ruled from Donegal Castle, with a strong fleet, Scottish mercenaries and learned bardic families such as the O'Clerys. Franciscan Donegal Friary was a key patron foundation.
kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.e: Red Hugh O'Donnell joined Hugh O'Neill in the Nine Years' War against England. After defeat, Rory O'Donnell, Earl of Tyrconnell, left Ireland in the Flight of the Earls in 1607, and his lands were confiscated for the Plantation of Ulster under the Kingdom of Ireland.

kingdom-of-the-algarve.t: Portugal's southern coast, held as a nominally separate kingdom by the Portuguese crown from its conquest until 1910.
kingdom-of-the-algarve.o: Afonso III of Portugal completed the conquest of the Algarve by taking Faro in 1249. Castile disputed the territory until the Treaty of Badajoz of 1267, after which Portuguese kings styled themselves Kings of Portugal and the Algarve.
kingdom-of-the-algarve.r: The Algarve had no separate institutions: it was governed from Lisbon as part of the Kingdom of Portugal, though its title and arms were kept as a mark of conquest. Its ports, especially Lagos, served as bases for Henry the Navigator's voyages to Africa. Fishing, salt, figs and almonds sustained its economy.
kingdom-of-the-algarve.e: The title was later expanded under Manuel I to cover territories in Africa. The Kingdom of the Algarve ended in law with the Portuguese monarchy in the revolution of 1910 and became a region of the First Portuguese Republic.

kingdom-of-bernicia.t: The northern Anglian kingdom based on the fortress of Bamburgh, whose kings united with Deira to create Northumbria.
kingdom-of-bernicia.o: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle dates Bernicia to 547, when Ida took the kingship and built Bamburgh. Its people were Angles who settled the coast between the Tees and the Forth among the British population. The British name Bryneich suggests the kingdom took over an earlier British territory.
kingdom-of-bernicia.r: Bernicia's kings were warriors whose power rested on tribute and plunder. Aethelfrith defeated Aedan of Dal Riata at Degsastan in 603 and the Britons at Chester, then seized Deira. His son Oswald brought Aidan from Iona, who founded Lindisfarne in 635, and royal sites such as Yeavering show grand halls.
kingdom-of-bernicia.e: Under Oswiu, Bernicia and the Kingdom of Deira were joined permanently after 654, forming the Kingdom of Northumbria. Bamburgh remained a royal fortress and later the seat of the Earldom of Bamburgh.

knossos.t: Leading city-state of Iron Age Crete on the site of the great Minoan palace, rival of Gortyn until the Roman conquest of 67 BCE.
knossos.o: Knossos survived the fall of its Bronze Age palace as a town and grew again in the early Iron Age. By the 7th century BCE it was a Dorian-speaking polis and, with Gortyn, one of the two strongest cities of Crete. The Minoan past was remembered in myths of Minos and the Labyrinth.
knossos.r: Like other Cretan cities, Knossos was ruled by annual magistrates called kosmoi, with men's messes and citizen training. The seer Epimenides was said to come from Knossos. Its coins showed the Labyrinth and the Minotaur. In the Hellenistic period Knossos fought Gortyn and Lyttos, destroying Lyttos in 220 BCE, and took part in the Cretan Koinon.
knossos.e: Rome conquered Crete under Quintus Caecilius Metellus between 69 and 67 BCE. Gortyn became the provincial capital, while Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony under Augustus. The Palace State of Knossos is described separately.

kingdom-of-loigis.t: Irish midland kingdom of the O'Mores, centred on the Rock of Dunamase, which fought the English until the plantation of Laois in 1556.
kingdom-of-loigis.o: The Loígis were a people of the Irish midlands in what is now County Laois, which takes its name from them. Tradition claimed they had won their lands as warriors serving the kings of the Kingdom of Leinster, and they formed a subject kingdom of Leinster from the early medieval period. From the 11th century their ruling family was the Uí Mórda, O'More.
kingdom-of-loigis.r: The kingdom was a land of bog, woodland and pasture, defended by its terrain. The Rock of Dunamase was a royal stronghold before the Anglo-Normans took it in the late 12th century and built a castle there. From the 14th century the O'Mores regained much of their territory, raiding the English Pale and living by cattle and the tribute of their followers.
kingdom-of-loigis.e: Under Mary I the English government confiscated Laois and Offaly and in 1556 created Queen's County, planted with English settlers around Maryborough, today Portlaoise. The O'Mores resisted for decades, notably under Rory Óg O'More, but their kingdom was ended.
kingdom-of-loigis.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-athamania.t: Small mountain kingdom on the borders of Epirus and Thessaly whose king Amynander played the Roman, Macedonian and Seleucid powers off against each other.
kingdom-of-athamania.o: The Athamanians were a people of the Pindus mountains around the upper Achelous, between Epirus, Thessaly and Aetolia. Little is known of their early history. Under Macedonian and Epirote dominance they had their own kings, and the kingdom became visible in the later 3rd century BCE, with its royal seat at Argithea.
kingdom-of-athamania.r: Athamania was a pastoral highland realm of villages and fortified hilltop towns. Its importance came from its position on routes between Thessaly and western Greece. King Amynander joined Rome against Philip V of Macedon in 200-197 BCE and acted as an intermediary, then sided with Antiochus III in 191 BCE.
kingdom-of-athamania.e: Philip V overran Athamania in 191 BCE and Amynander fled to Ambracia. With Aetolian help he recovered his kingdom in 189 BCE, but it disappears from the record soon after and was absorbed into its neighbours. Knowledge of it comes almost entirely from Polybius and Livy.

kingdom-of-holland.t: Napoleon's client kingdom for his brother Louis, who tried to rule as a Dutch king and was removed for defending his subjects.
kingdom-of-holland.o: In 1806 Napoleon replaced the Batavian Republic with a kingdom and installed his brother Louis Bonaparte as king. Louis learned Dutch, made Amsterdam the capital and turned its town hall into a royal palace.
kingdom-of-holland.r: Louis founded the Royal Institute and a national museum, introduced a civil code and took a sympathetic line toward Dutch interests. He resisted conscription and enforced the Continental System only loosely, which allowed smuggling with Britain. The economy suffered nonetheless, and the British landed on Walcheren in 1809.
kingdom-of-holland.e: Napoleon, angry at Louis's independence, forced him to abdicate in July 1810, and the kingdom was annexed to the French Empire. French rule ended in 1813, leading to the Sovereign Principality of the United Netherlands.

kingdom-of-arles.t: The united kingdom of Burgundy and Provence, stretching from Basel to the Mediterranean, that became the third crown of the Holy Roman emperors.
kingdom-of-arles.o: Around 933 Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy acquired the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy from Hugh of Arles, uniting the lands between the Jura and the Mediterranean. His son Conrad the Peaceful ruled from 937 to 993 under the protection of Otto I, who had taken the young king to his court.
kingdom-of-arles.r: Royal power was weak: counts, archbishops of Lyon, Vienne and Arles, and later lords such as the dauphins of Viennois and counts of Provence held real authority. When the childless Rudolf III died in 1032, the kingdom passed to Emperor Conrad II. Frederick Barbarossa was crowned at Arles in 1178 and Charles IV in 1365.
kingdom-of-arles.e: French influence grew steadily along the Rhône. In 1378 Charles IV made the French Dauphin, the future Charles VI, imperial vicar of the kingdom for life, effectively ending imperial rule there. Its lands were gradually absorbed by the Kingdom of France and Savoy.

kingdom-of-lysimachus.t: Short-lived Hellenistic kingdom of Alexander's general Lysimachus, ruling Thrace, Macedon and western Asia Minor before his death at Corupedium.
kingdom-of-lysimachus.o: After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, Lysimachus received Thrace as his satrapy and spent years subduing the Odrysian Kingdom under Seuthes III. In 309 BCE he founded Lysimachia on the Gallipoli peninsula as his capital, and around 306 BCE he took the royal title with the other Successors.
kingdom-of-lysimachus.r: Lysimachus was a careful financier who built a large treasury and minted famous tetradrachms showing the deified Alexander. After the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE he gained most of western Asia Minor, refounding Ephesus. North of the Haemus he campaigned against the Getae, and around 292 BCE was captured by their king Dromichaetes. In 288 BCE he and Pyrrhus took Macedon, which he held alone from 285 BCE.
kingdom-of-lysimachus.e: Family murders, including the killing of his son Agathocles, alienated his supporters. Seleucus I defeated and killed him at Corupedium in 281 BCE. His realm broke up, and Thrace soon fell to the Celtic invasions and the Kingdom of Tylis.
