kingdom-of-the-isles.t: A Norse-Gaelic sea kingdom of Man and the Hebrides, ruled from the Isle of Man by the Crovan dynasty under Norwegian overlordship.
kingdom-of-the-isles.o: Godred Crovan, a Norse-Gael who had fought at Stamford Bridge in 1066, seized the Isle of Man in 1079 after a battle at Sky Hill. His descendants ruled Man and the Hebrides, the Sudreys, as a kingdom under the nominal overlordship of Norway.
kingdom-of-the-isles.r: The kingdom was a maritime power of galleys and island fortresses, with Castle Rushen and the church at Rushen Abbey. Man's Tynwald assembly descends from its Norse institutions. Its kings intervened in Irish and Scottish affairs. Somerled's revolt in 1156 took the southern Hebrides, leaving the Crovan line with Man, Lewis and Skye.
kingdom-of-the-isles.e: After the Battle of Largs in 1263, Norway ceded Man and the Isles to the Kingdom of Scotland by the Treaty of Perth in 1266, the year after the last king, Magnus Olafsson, died. Man later came under English rule as the Lordship of Mann.

kingdom-of-salamis.t: The leading city-kingdom of ancient Cyprus, whose king Evagoras I united much of the island and defied the Persian Empire for a decade.
kingdom-of-salamis.o: Salamis was founded on the east coast of Cyprus in the 11th century BCE, succeeding nearby Enkomi as its harbour silted up. Greek tradition named Teucer, brother of Ajax, as its founder. Its royal tombs of the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, with chariots and sacrificed horses, recall Homeric burial customs.
kingdom-of-salamis.r: The kings of Salamis were often the most powerful on Cyprus. Evelthon struck the island's first coins in the 6th century BCE, and Onesilus led the Cypriot revolt against Persia in 498 BCE. Evagoras I, who reigned from 411 to 374 BCE, promoted Greek culture, allied with Athens and fought the Achaemenid Empire until a negotiated peace in 380 BCE.
kingdom-of-salamis.e: The last king, Nicocreon, allied with Ptolemy I and died c. 310 BCE, and in 306 BCE Demetrius Poliorcetes won a great naval battle off Salamis. The kingdom then passed under the Ptolemaic Empire. Salamis remained a major city, renamed Constantia, until abandoned after the Arab raids of the 7th century CE.

kingdom-of-leinster.t: Province-kingdom of south-east Ireland, whose exiled king Diarmait Mac Murchada invited the Anglo-Normans in and so opened eight centuries of English involvement.
kingdom-of-leinster.o: The Laigin, the people of Leinster, appear in the earliest Irish traditions as a major power whose kings once held the midlands and Tara. From the 5th century the rising Uí Néill drove them south, and Leinster settled into an over-kingdom covering most of the south-east, contested between dynasties such as the Uí Dúnlainge in the north and the Ui Chennselaig in the south.
kingdom-of-leinster.r: Kings ruled through tribute and alliances with subject peoples, and great monasteries such as Kildare, Glendalough and Ferns flourished. Brandub mac Echach defeated the high king at Dún Bolg in 598. Viking Dublin lay within Leinster, and from the 11th century its kings sought to control it; Diarmait mac Máel na mBó, who died in 1072, ruled Dublin and nearly became high king.
kingdom-of-leinster.e: In 1166 Diarmait Mac Murchada was expelled and sought help from Henry II. Anglo-Norman knights led by Strongbow, who married Diarmait's daughter Aoife, took Wexford, Waterford and Dublin. On Diarmait's death in 1171 Strongbow claimed Leinster, and Henry II's arrival brought it under the English crown.

kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.t: The kingdom of Provence founded by Boso in 879, the first realm in the Carolingian West to elect a king from outside the Carolingian family.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.o: In 879, after the death of Louis the Stammerer, bishops and nobles meeting at Mantaille elected Boso, a brother-in-law of Charles the Bald, as king of the lands around Vienne, Lyon and Provence. The Carolingian kings besieged Vienne in 880–882, but Boso's family kept control of the Rhône valley.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.r: The kingdom was a loose union of counties along the Rhône and in Provence, governed from Vienne with strong support from the bishops. Boso's son Louis the Blind was crowned emperor in Rome in 901 but was captured and blinded by Berengar of Italy in 905. Afterwards real power lay with his kinsman Hugh of Arles.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.e: Hugh of Arles, busy with his ambitions as king of Italy, gave up his claims to Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy around 933. The two Burgundian kingdoms were then united as the Kingdom of Arles, which later passed to the Holy Roman Empire.

kingdom-of-navarre.t: The Basque Pyrenean kingdom of Pamplona, which under Sancho III dominated Christian Spain and survived in part until 1841.
kingdom-of-navarre.o: Around 824, after the Basques defeated a Frankish army at the second Battle of Roncevaux, Íñigo Arista became ruler of Pamplona, allied with his kinsmen the Banu Qasi. In 905 Sancho Garcés I founded the Jimena dynasty and pushed south into the Ebro valley and La Rioja.
kingdom-of-navarre.r: Sancho III the Great, from 1004 to 1035, controlled Aragon, Castile and the Pyrenean counties, the dominant power of Christian Iberia. After a period of partition between 1076 and 1134, the kingdom revived. Sancho VII fought at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. French dynasties ruled from 1234, and Charles III the Noble built the palace of Olite. Basque, Romance and Latin were spoken, and the kingdom kept its own fueros and cortes.
kingdom-of-navarre.e: In 1512 Ferdinand the Catholic conquered Upper Navarre, joined to Castile in 1515, while Lower Navarre north of the Pyrenees remained with the Albret family. Its kings became kings of France in 1589. Spanish Navarre kept its own institutions until the law of 1841 made it a province.

kingdom-of-sicily.t: Southern Italy's Norman kingdom, famed for its Arab-Byzantine-Latin court culture, which after 1282 continued as the island realm of Sicily until 1816.
kingdom-of-sicily.o: Roger II, ruler of the County of Sicily and the Duchy of Apulia and Calabria, obtained a royal title from Antipope Anacletus II and was crowned in Palermo on Christmas Day 1130. The kingdom united Sicily and the Italian south, including the former principalities of Capua and Bari.
kingdom-of-sicily.r: The Norman kings ran a centralised state with Arabic, Greek and Latin chanceries, and built the Palatine Chapel, Cefalù and Monreale. Through marriage it passed to the Hohenstaufen: Frederick II issued the Constitutions of Melfi in 1231. Charles of Anjou took it in 1266, but the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 brought Peter III of Aragon to the island, leaving the mainland as the Kingdom of Naples.
kingdom-of-sicily.e: The island kingdom passed to Aragon and Habsburg Spain under viceroys, then briefly to Savoy in 1713, to Austria in 1720 and to the Bourbons in 1735. In 1816 Ferdinand merged it with Naples to form the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.t: The realm created by Alfred the Great and his son Edward, joining Wessex and English Mercia into the direct ancestor of the Kingdom of England.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.o: In 886 Alfred occupied London and, according to the Chronicle, all the English not under the Danes submitted to him. His charters began to use the title king of the Anglo-Saxons, uniting the Kingdom of Wessex with western Mercia under Aethelred, Lord of the Mercians, who married Alfred's daughter Aethelflaed.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.r: The kingdom was defended by burhs and a reorganised army. Alfred issued a law code and sponsored translations of Latin works into English. Edward the Elder and Aethelflaed reconquered the southern Danelaw, including the Five Boroughs and Danish East Anglia, between 910 and 920.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.e: After Aethelflaed's death Edward absorbed Mercia in 918. In 927 his son Aethelstan took York and received the submission of northern rulers, becoming the first king of the Kingdom of England.

kos.t: Dorian island state off Anatolia, birthplace of Hippocrates and home of the famous healing sanctuary of Asclepius.
kos.o: Kos, an island off the Carian coast near Halicarnassus, was settled from the Bronze Age, with Mycenaean remains. Dorian Greeks occupied it in the early Iron Age, and it joined the Dorian Hexapolis with Knidos, Halicarnassus and the Rhodian cities. Its first chief town was Astypalaia in the south-west.
kos.r: Kos was known for wine and fine translucent silk cloth. Hippocrates was born there c. 460 BCE and the Coan school of medicine bears his name. After Persian rule the island joined the Delian League. In 366 BCE the Coans founded a new capital on the north-east tip, and the Asclepieion was later built nearby.
kos.e: Kos was a favoured base of the Ptolemaic Empire, where Ptolemy II was born and the poet Philitas taught. It later allied with Rome and became part of the province of Asia in 129 BCE, remaining a free city prized for its sanctuary.

kingdom-of-paris.t: Merovingian kingdom centred on Paris, created when Clovis' realm was divided among his sons in 511.
kingdom-of-paris.o: On the death of Clovis in 511 the Kingdom of the Franks was shared among his four sons. Childebert I received the lands around Paris, together with the Channel coast and later parts of Aquitaine and Burgundy.
kingdom-of-paris.r: Childebert ruled for nearly fifty years, campaigning against the Kingdom of the Burgundians and the Visigoths in Spain, from where he brought back relics of Saint Vincent. For them he founded the abbey later called Saint-Germain-des-Prés. He joined his brother Chlothar I in murdering their nephews, the sons of Chlodomer of Orléans.
kingdom-of-paris.e: Childebert died without sons in 558, and Chlothar I briefly reunited the Frankish lands. In 561 Paris passed to Chlothar's son Charibert I, and after Charibert's death in 567 his kingdom was divided among his brothers, with Paris shared between them.

kingdom-of-paphos.t: Ancient Cypriot kingdom centred on the great sanctuary of Aphrodite, whose kings served as the goddess's high priests for some eight centuries.
kingdom-of-paphos.o: Paphos grew at Palaepaphos, modern Kouklia, a Late Bronze Age town in south-west Cyprus. In the 12th and 11th centuries BCE Aegean settlers arrived, and Greek legend credited Agapenor of Tegea with founding the city after the Trojan War. An inscription of the 11th century BCE shows Greek already written there.
kingdom-of-paphos.r: Its kings combined royal power with the priesthood of the Paphian goddess, later identified with Aphrodite, whose open-air sanctuary with a conical stone drew pilgrims from across the Mediterranean. Paphos used the Cypriot syllabary for Greek and struck its own coins. It paid tribute to Assyria and later to the Achaemenid Empire, and joined the revolt against Persia in 498 BCE.
kingdom-of-paphos.e: The last king, Nicocles, founded the harbour city of Nea Paphos, which became the capital of Ptolemaic and Roman Cyprus. The kingdom was abolished when Ptolemy I took the island, by c. 306 BCE, but the sanctuary of Aphrodite flourished into late antiquity.

kingdom-of-ui-maine.t: Kingdom of the O'Kellys in east Galway and south Roscommon, one of the largest subject kingdoms of Connacht, which lasted until the Composition of 1585.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.o: The Uí Maine claimed descent from Maine Mór, said to have won lands west of the Shannon in the 5th century. By the early medieval period they held a large kingdom in what is now east County Galway and south Roscommon, within the over-kingdom of the Kingdom of Connacht, with privileges of their own.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.r: Their kings, from the 10th century the Ua Cellaig, O'Kelly, served the kings of Connacht in war and sometimes contested the kingship. Tadhg Mór Ua Cellaig fell fighting for Brian Bóruma at Clontarf in 1014. The O'Kellys were famous patrons of learning: Uilliam Buidhe Ó Ceallaigh held a great Christmas feast for the poets of Ireland in 1351, and the Book of Uí Maine was compiled for the family.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.e: Anglo-Norman lords, especially the de Burghs, took part of Uí Maine in the 13th century, but the O'Kellys kept much of it. Under the Composition of Connacht in 1585 their lordship was converted into crown tenure, ending the kingdom's independent status.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-east-anglia.t: The kingdom of the East Angles in Norfolk and Suffolk, famed for the Sutton Hoo ship burial and for its martyred last king, Edmund.
kingdom-of-east-anglia.o: Angles settled Norfolk and Suffolk in the 5th century, and the Wuffingas dynasty, named after Wuffa, ruled by the 6th century. Its royal centre lay at Rendlesham in the Deben valley, close to the burial ground at Sutton Hoo.
kingdom-of-east-anglia.r: Raedwald, overlord of the southern English around 616, probably lies in the Sutton Hoo ship burial, with its gold and Byzantine silver. He kept both a Christian altar and a pagan one. Later kings founded the bishopric at Dunwich under Felix and monasteries such as Ely. Ipswich became one of the first post-Roman towns.
kingdom-of-east-anglia.e: East Anglia was often under Mercian overlordship in the 8th century. The Great Heathen Army killed King Edmund in 869 and the Danes later settled the land as the Danish Kingdom of East Anglia. Edmund's cult grew at Bury St Edmunds.

kingdom-of-alashiya.t: Late Bronze Age kingdom on Cyprus whose rulers traded copper with Egypt, the Hittites and Ugarit, as revealed by the Amarna letters.
kingdom-of-alashiya.o: Alashiya appears in Near Eastern texts from the 18th century BCE as a source of copper, and most scholars identify it with Cyprus or part of it. Cyprus developed urban centres in the Late Cypriot period from c. 1650 BCE, including Enkomi on the east coast, Kalavasos and Alassa, though which was the royal seat is uncertain.
kingdom-of-alashiya.r: The king of Alashiya corresponded with Pharaoh Akhenaten as a 'brother' in the Amarna letters, sending copper ingots in return for silver, oil and luxury goods. Clay analysis shows these letters were made on Cyprus. Enkomi had copper workshops and ashlar buildings, and the island used the Cypro-Minoan script. The Hittite Empire claimed overlordship in the 13th century BCE.
kingdom-of-alashiya.e: Letters from Ugarit describe enemy ships threatening Alashiya c. 1200 BCE, and Suppiluliuma II fought naval battles off its coast. In the following century Cypriot towns declined or moved, Aegean settlers arrived, and the island reorganised into the Iron Age kingdoms such as Salamis, Paphos and Kition.

kingdom-of-castile.t: The medieval kingdom of Castile, which took Toledo, crushed the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa and became the dominant power of Christian Iberia.
kingdom-of-castile.o: The County of Castile had been raised to a kingdom by Ferdinand I, who also ruled the Kingdom of León. At his death in 1065 he divided his realms, leaving Castile to his eldest son Sancho II. After Sancho's murder in 1072 his brother Alfonso VI reunited Castile and León.
kingdom-of-castile.r: Castile was a frontier society of free settlers, town councils with their own fueros and mounted warriors, later organised in military orders such as Calatrava and Santiago. Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085. Alfonso VIII, defeated at Alarcos in 1195, led the coalition that destroyed the Almohad army at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. Burgos, on the pilgrim road to Santiago, prospered on trade and wool.
kingdom-of-castile.e: Castile and León were separated again from 1157, but in 1230 Ferdinand III, already king of Castile, inherited León, creating the lasting union known as the Crown of Castile, which absorbed most of al-Andalus within a generation.

kingdom-of-desmond.t: The MacCarthy kingdom of South Munster, created when Munster was split in 1118 and surviving in parts until the end of the 16th century.
kingdom-of-desmond.o: The Treaty of Glanmire in 1118 divided Munster, giving the south, Deasmumu, to the MacCarthys, heirs of the Eoganacht kings of Cashel. Cormac MacCarthy ruled from Cork and built Cormac's Chapel on the Rock of Cashel, consecrated in 1134.
kingdom-of-desmond.r: Desmond's kings lost much of Cork to the Normans after 1177, but Finghin MacCarthy's victory at Callann in 1261 halted the colonists. The MacCarthy Mor branch then ruled from Pallis in Kerry, with cadet lines in Carbery and Muskerry. The kingdom was an overlordship of Gaelic lords such as the O'Sullivans and O'Donoghues.
kingdom-of-desmond.e: Donal MacCarthy Mor became Earl of Clancare in 1565 under the Kingdom of Ireland. His death without a legitimate male heir in 1596 ended the senior line, and its lands passed into English plantations.

kingdom-of-eile.t: Irish kingdom of the O'Carrolls around Birr, on the border of Munster and Leinster, which survived as Ely O'Carroll until the 16th century.
kingdom-of-eile.o: Éile was the territory of an early medieval people of the Irish midlands, in what is now south Offaly and north Tipperary, counted as part of the Kingdom of Munster. Its ruling family claimed descent from the Eóganachta's kin, and from the 11th century the Ua Cerbaill, O'Carroll, became the dominant line, giving the region its later name of Ely O'Carroll.
kingdom-of-eile.r: The kingdom lay on the boundary between Munster and Leinster, which gave it strategic value and exposed it to raids. The monastery of Birr, founded by St Brendan of Birr in the 6th century, produced the Book of MacRegol, an illuminated gospel book of about 800. The O'Carrolls ruled from strongholds such as Leap Castle and Birr.
kingdom-of-eile.e: Anglo-Norman settlers took part of the territory in the 13th century, but the O'Carrolls recovered much of it. In 1552 their chief Tadhg O'Carroll surrendered his lands to the crown and was created Baron of Ely, and the region was later divided between King's County and Tipperary.
kingdom-of-eile.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-the-netherlands.t: The Dutch constitutional monarchy, shaped by the 1848 constitution, colonial empire, neutrality, war and post-war reconstruction into a founding EU member.
kingdom-of-the-netherlands.o: The Kingdom of the Netherlands took its present shape when William I accepted Belgian independence in the Treaty of London of 1839. Constitutional revision in 1848, drafted under Johan Rudolf Thorbecke, introduced ministerial responsibility and direct elections, establishing parliamentary government.
kingdom-of-the-netherlands.r: The colonial empire, above all the Dutch East Indies, brought wealth through the cultivation system, criticised in Multatuli's Max Havelaar. Society was organised in 'pillars' of Protestants, Catholics, socialists and liberals. The country stayed neutral in the First World War but was occupied by Germany from 1940 to 1945, while Queen Wilhelmina led the government from London.
kingdom-of-the-netherlands.e: Indonesia became independent in 1949. After the North Sea flood of 1953 the Delta Works were built. The Netherlands co-founded NATO and the European Communities, and since 1954 the Kingdom has included Caribbean countries. Willem-Alexander became king in 2013.

kingdom-of-the-regni.t: Client kingdom of Togidubnus in Sussex and Hampshire, a loyal ally of Rome after the conquest whose seat may have been the palace at Fishbourne.
kingdom-of-the-regni.o: After the Roman invasion of 43, much of the former realm of the Atrebates (Britain) was entrusted to Togidubnus, a British noble loyal to Rome. Tacitus says that certain states were given to him and that he remained faithful down to his own day, and the region became a base for Roman operations along the south coast.
kingdom-of-the-regni.r: An inscription from Chichester dedicating a temple to Neptune and Minerva names Tiberius Claudius Togidubnus as great king in Britain, showing that he held Roman citizenship and royal status. His capital, Noviomagus Reginorum, grew into a Roman-style town, and the lavish villa at Fishbourne, with mosaics and formal gardens, has often been linked to him. The kingdom provided Rome with a stable and Romanised territory.
kingdom-of-the-regni.e: When Togidubnus died, probably around 80, the client kingdom was absorbed into the province of Roman Britain. Its lands were divided into civitates, the Regni around Chichester and probably the Belgae (Britain) around Winchester. Chichester remains the main town of the region.

kingdom-of-the-heruli.t: A short-lived East Germanic kingdom on the middle Danube, briefly dominant over the Lombards before a crushing defeat around 508.
kingdom-of-the-heruli.o: The Heruli had been in the Black Sea region and under Hunnic rule; after the Huns' collapse following the Battle of Nedao in 454, one group settled near the middle Danube, probably in southern Moravia, western Slovakia and Lower Austria. By about 490 they had a strong kingdom that took tribute from the Lombards.
kingdom-of-the-heruli.r: Procopius describes the Heruli as fierce warriors who kept old pagan customs, including the sacrifice of elderly people and the suicide of widows. Their king Rodulf allied with Theodoric the Great, who adopted him as a 'son in arms' around 507. The kingdom rested on warrior power and tribute rather than settled institutions.
kingdom-of-the-heruli.e: Around 508 Rodulf attacked the Lombards under Tato and was killed in a heavy defeat. The Heruli scattered: some moved into Roman territory and became federates in Illyricum, others went to Scandinavia according to Procopius. Herul soldiers later fought for Justinian in Italy and Persia.

kingdom-of-cottius.t: Alpine client kingdom around Susa whose ruler Cottius allied with Augustus and gave his name to the Cottian Alps.
kingdom-of-cottius.o: In the 1st century BCE the Segusini and neighbouring Alpine peoples around the Mont Genèvre pass were ruled by a king named Donnus, who appears in Caesar's time. His son, Marcus Julius Cottius, chose to make peace with Augustus rather than resist the Roman conquest of the Alps.
kingdom-of-cottius.r: Cottius governed fourteen Alpine communities as a Roman prefect while keeping royal status locally. He built and maintained the road over the Mont Genèvre pass, a key route between Italy and Gaul. In 9–8 BCE he erected the Arch of Augustus at Segusio (Susa), whose inscription lists his peoples. The kingdom combined Celtic traditions with Roman administration.
kingdom-of-cottius.e: Claudius restored the royal title to Cottius's son, Marcus Julius Cottius II, in 44 CE. When he died without an heir around 63 CE, Nero annexed the kingdom as the province of the Alpes Cottiae. The name survives in the Cottian Alps.

kingdom-of-moylurg.t: A Gaelic lordship of north Roscommon ruled by the MacDermots from their island fortress on Lough Key.
kingdom-of-moylurg.o: Magh Luirg was the territory of a branch of the Sil Muiredaig, the ruling kindred of Connacht. In the 12th century the MacDermot family, descended from Diarmait mac Taidg, emerged as its rulers and as marshals of the O'Connor kings of Connacht.
kingdom-of-moylurg.r: The MacDermots ruled from the Rock of Lough Ce, an island fortress on Lough Key, and patronised the abbey of Boyle and the learned families who compiled the Annals of Loch Ce. Their lordship was based on cattle, clients and armed retainers, and they served as kingmakers in Connacht politics.
kingdom-of-moylurg.e: The Composition of Connacht in 1585 brought the lordship under English land law. The MacDermots kept part of their lands and their title, the MacDermot, Prince of Coolavin, has been recognised into modern times.

kingdom-of-lapethos.t: North Cypriot kingdom where Phoenician kings ruled a Greek population in the Classical age, until Ptolemy I deposed the last king in 312 BCE.
kingdom-of-lapethos.o: Lapethos lay on the north coast of Cyprus near modern Lambousa, facing Anatolia. Greek tradition said it was founded by Praxandros from Laconia after the Trojan War. A city-kingdom by the 7th century BCE, it had close ties with the Phoenician coast.
kingdom-of-lapethos.r: In the 5th and 4th centuries BCE Lapethos was ruled by a dynasty with Phoenician names, such as Sidqmelek, who issued coins with Phoenician legends; Phoenician inscriptions from the town honour Melqart and other gods. The economy rested on farming, fishing and trade, and the city had a good harbour.
kingdom-of-lapethos.e: Its last king, Praxippos, supported Antigonus against Ptolemy I, who removed him in 312 BCE and annexed the kingdom. Lapethos continued as a Ptolemaic and Roman town, later called Lambousa, abandoned after Arab raids in the 7th century CE.

kingdom-of-pylos.t: Mycenaean kingdom of Messenia whose burnt palace preserved more than a thousand Linear B tablets, the fullest record of a Bronze Age Greek state.
kingdom-of-pylos.o: Pylos grew on the Englianos ridge in western Messenia, where rich shaft and tholos tombs show an emerging elite by c. 1650 BCE, including the Griffin Warrior burial found in 2015. By the 14th and 13th centuries BCE its rulers had unified Messenia into a single kingdom divided into two provinces.
kingdom-of-pylos.r: The palace, linked by Homer with King Nestor, was headed by a wanax with a lawagetas below him. Its Linear B archive records taxation of some 16 districts, landholding, bronze-smiths, flax and perfumed oil production, rowers for the fleet and offerings to Poseidon, Zeus, Hera and the Potnia. Frescoes and a well-preserved throne room survive.
kingdom-of-pylos.e: The palace was destroyed by fire c. 1180 BCE, apparently while preparing coastal defences, and the region largely depopulated. Its tablets, baked by the fire, were found by Carl Blegen in 1939 and helped Michael Ventris show in 1952 that Linear B was Greek.

kingdom-of-circinn.t: A Pictish kingdom or province in the area of Angus and the Mearns, named in early Irish annals and in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne.
kingdom-of-circinn.o: Circinn appears as one of the seven Pictish provinces in the origin legend that named them after the sons of Cruithne, and in Irish annals, which record a battle of Circinn in 598. It is usually placed in Angus and the Mearns, south of the Mounth.
kingdom-of-circinn.r: Almost nothing is known of its government. It was probably one of the regional lordships within the Pictish kingdom, and the fertile lowlands of Angus held important church sites such as Aberlemno and later Brechin, with their carved Pictish stones.
kingdom-of-circinn.e: Circinn's identity merged into the Kingdom of Scotland when Pictland became Alba in the 9th and 10th centuries. The later earldoms of Angus and the Mearns may continue its territory.

kingdom-of-mycenae.t: The leading Bronze Age Greek kingdom in the Argolid, whose shaft graves, Lion Gate and tholos tombs gave its name to the Mycenaean civilisation.
kingdom-of-mycenae.o: Mycenae occupies a hill in the north-east Argolid controlling routes to Corinth. Its rise is shown by Grave Circles A and B, used c. 1650 to 1500 BCE, with gold masks and weapons. In the 14th and 13th centuries BCE a palace, Cyclopean walls and great tholos tombs such as the Treasury of Atreus were built.
kingdom-of-mycenae.r: Mycenae was ruled by a wanax from a palace with a central megaron and frescoes, and was probably the most powerful of several Argolid centres including Tiryns. Linear B tablets record perfumed oil and other goods. Its pottery spread across the Mediterranean, and some scholars link it to the Ahhiyawa known from Hittite texts. The Lion Gate dates to c. 1250 BCE.
kingdom-of-mycenae.e: The citadel suffered destructions c. 1200 BCE and the palace system collapsed, though occupation continued until c. 1100 BCE. Later the small town was destroyed by Argos c. 468 BCE. Homer made it the seat of Agamemnon, and Schliemann's excavations from 1876 made it famous.

kingdom-of-cologne.t: Kingdom of the Rhineland Franks at Cologne, absorbed by Clovis through murder around 509.
kingdom-of-cologne.o: The Franks of the middle Rhine, later called Ripuarian Franks, took over Cologne in the mid 5th century as Roman power collapsed. By the late 5th century they had their own king, Sigibert, who ruled from the former Roman capital of Germania Inferior.
kingdom-of-cologne.r: Sigibert, called the Lame from a wound received fighting the Alemanni at Zülpich, was an ally of Clovis and sent his son Chloderic to fight the Visigoths at Vouillé in 507. The Ripuarian Franks kept their own law, the Lex Ripuaria, written down in the 7th century.
kingdom-of-cologne.e: Gregory of Tours relates that Clovis incited Chloderic to murder his father, then had Chloderic killed and was raised on a shield as king by the people of Cologne, around 509. The realm became part of the Kingdom of the Franks and later of Austrasia.

kingdom-of-kent.t: The first English kingdom to accept Christianity, under Æthelberht in 597, and the home of the earliest laws written in English.
kingdom-of-kent.o: Bede says Kent was settled by Jutes led by Hengest and Horsa, who came as mercenaries of Vortigern around 449 and then turned against the Britons. The story is legendary, but archaeology shows strong links with Jutland and Frankish Gaul by the 6th century. The kingdom took its name from the British Cantiaci, and its centre was Canterbury.
kingdom-of-kent.r: Æthelberht, king from about 589 to 616, married the Frankish Christian princess Bertha and in 597 received Augustine's mission from Pope Gregory, making Canterbury the seat of the English Church. His law code is the earliest document in English. Kent was rich from trade with Francia, producing fine garnet jewellery and gold coinage, and later kings such as Wihtred issued further laws.
kingdom-of-kent.e: From the 760s Kent fell under Offa of Mercia; a revolt by Eadberht Præn was crushed in 798. In 825 Egbert of Wessex took Kent, which was ruled as a sub-kingdom by West Saxon princes until it was merged into Wessex in the 860s, later becoming an English shire.

kingdom-of-deheubarth.t: The kingdom of south-west Wales, founded by Hywel Dda and later led by the Lord Rhys, a centre of Welsh law, poetry and resistance to Norman conquest.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.o: Deheubarth, 'the southern part', was formed around 920 when Hywel Dda united his inheritance of the Kingdom of Seisyllwg with Dyfed. Hywel later also ruled Gwynedd and Powys, and became the only Welsh king to issue coins.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.r: Hywel was credited with codifying Welsh law, the Cyfraith Hywel, which governed inheritance, compensation and status. The kingdom's centre was Dinefwr in the Tywi valley. Norman lords overran much of it after 1093, but Rhys ap Gruffydd, the Lord Rhys, rebuilt its power, held the first recorded eisteddfod at Cardigan in 1176 and patronised Strata Florida Abbey.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.e: After the Lord Rhys died in 1197, his sons divided Deheubarth in bitter feuds. Its remnants came under Gwynedd's Principality of Wales, and its lands were absorbed by the English crown after 1283.

kingdom-of-majorca.t: A Christian kingdom created after James I's conquest of Majorca, independent under its own dynasty from 1276 to 1344 and a realm of Aragon thereafter.
kingdom-of-majorca.o: James I of Aragon conquered Majorca from the Almohads in 1229, then Ibiza in 1235, and established a separate kingdom. On his death in 1276 he left Majorca, Roussillon, Cerdanya and Montpellier to his younger son James II, creating an independent dynasty.
kingdom-of-majorca.r: The kingdom was a Mediterranean trading state, with Palma and Perpignan as royal seats, merchant fleets reaching North Africa and a famed school of cartographers who made the Catalan Atlas. Ramon Llull, philosopher and missionary, was its most famous son. Its kings were forced to accept vassalage to the Crown of Aragon.
kingdom-of-majorca.e: Peter IV of Aragon seized the kingdom in 1343-1344, and James III was killed at Llucmajor in 1349 trying to retake it. Majorca remained a separate realm within the Crown until the Nueva Planta decree of 1715.

kingdom-of-the-burgundians.t: East Germanic kingdom of the Rhône and Saône valleys, whose destruction on the Rhine inspired the Nibelungenlied and whose laws shaped Burgundy.
kingdom-of-the-burgundians.o: The Burgundians crossed the Rhine in the early 5th century, and in 411 their king Gundahar set up a realm around Worms as Roman allies. In 436 the general Aetius had them crushed by Hunnic troops, a disaster remembered in the Nibelungenlied. In 443 the survivors were resettled in Sapaudia, around Geneva.
kingdom-of-the-burgundians.r: From there they spread across the Rhône and Saône valleys, ruling from Lyon and Geneva. King Gundobad issued a law code for his Burgundian subjects and another for Romans, and Burgundians and Gallo-Romans shared land. The kings were Arians, but Sigismund converted to Catholic Christianity.
kingdom-of-the-burgundians.e: Clovis' sons attacked them in 523, killing Sigismund. After a final defeat in 534 King Godomar disappeared and the land became part of the Kingdom of the Franks, later the Frankish Kingdom of Burgundy. The name Burgundy has endured for fifteen centuries.

kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.t: The Austrian-ruled kingdom of Lombardy and Venetia, centre of Habsburg power in Italy and target of the wars of Italian independence.
kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.o: In 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave Lombardy and the former Republic of Venice to the Austrian Empire, which joined them as a kingdom with the emperor as king, governed by a viceroy, at first Archduke Rainer.
kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.r: Lombardy-Venetia had an efficient administration, good schools and a prosperous economy, but censorship and police repression made Austria unpopular; the patriot Silvio Pellico described his imprisonment in the Spielberg fortress. In 1848 the Five Days of Milan and the Republic of San Marco drove out the Austrians, but Marshal Radetzky reconquered both. Archduke Maximilian tried liberal reforms as governor-general in 1857–1859.
kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.e: Defeat by France and the Kingdom of Sardinia at Solferino in 1859 cost Austria Lombardy. After the war of 1866, Venetia passed to the Kingdom of Italy.

kingdom-of-powys.t: Kingdom of mid and north-east Wales and the Marches that long faced Mercia across Offa's Dyke, until it split into two lordships after 1160.
kingdom-of-powys.o: Powys arose in the territory of the Cornovii after Roman rule ended around 410, its name perhaps from the Latin pagenses, country people. Its early kings claimed descent from Cadell Ddyrnllug and, according to the Pillar of Eliseg, from Vortigern and Magnus Maximus. Its first centre may have been at Wroxeter or Pengwern before the English advance pushed it westward.
kingdom-of-powys.r: Powys bordered the Mercians and suffered heavily from their expansion; Selyf ap Cynan fell at the battle of Chester around 615, and Offa built his dyke along the frontier in the 8th century. Cyngen ap Cadell raised the Pillar of Eliseg near Llangollen to honour an ancestor who won back land from the English. Later kings ruled from Mathrafal, and its society rested on cattle and kin-based law.
kingdom-of-powys.e: Cyngen died on pilgrimage to Rome in 854, and Powys passed to Rhodri the Great of the Kingdom of Gwynedd. A native dynasty returned under Bleddyn ap Cynfyn in the 1060s, but after Madog ap Maredudd died in 1160 the kingdom split into Powys Fadog and Powys Wenwynwyn.

kingdom-of-dunoding.t: Small early kingdom of north-west Wales, named in legend after a son of Cunedda, which became the cantrefi of Eifionydd and Ardudwy in Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-dunoding.o: According to Welsh genealogical tradition, Dunoding was named after Dunod, a son of Cunedda, who received the land as his share when Cunedda's family settled north Wales in the 5th century. Historians treat the Cunedda story as a later origin legend, but Dunoding existed as a distinct territory on the coast south of Snowdonia.
kingdom-of-dunoding.r: Little is recorded of its rulers or government. The kingdom comprised two districts, Eifionydd around Criccieth and Ardudwy around Harlech, a land of coastal farmland backed by mountains, rich in prehistoric monuments. It seems to have been ruled by a local branch of the dynasty of the Kingdom of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-dunoding.e: Dunoding was absorbed into the Kingdom of Gwynedd as two cantrefi, probably by the 10th century. Eifionydd and Ardudwy remained administrative districts, later guarded by the castles of Criccieth and Harlech after the English conquest of 1283.

kingdom-of-kourion.t: Cypriot kingdom on a clifftop above the south coast, remembered for the sanctuary of Apollo Hylates and for its king's betrayal at the Battle of Salamis in 497 BCE.
kingdom-of-kourion.o: Kourion arose in the Episkopi area of southern Cyprus, near a Late Bronze Age settlement, in the 11th century BCE. Its Greek inhabitants claimed descent from settlers from Argos. By the 7th century BCE it was one of the island's city-kingdoms, listed among the Cypriot rulers who paid tribute to the Assyrian king Esarhaddon.
kingdom-of-kourion.r: The kings ruled a fertile territory along the Kouris river. The sanctuary of Apollo Hylates, god of the woodland, was its chief cult centre, and rich tombs yielded the gold and silver of the so-called Kourion treasure. Kourion followed the Cypriot syllabary and Greek institutions, under Assyrian and then Achaemenid overlordship.
kingdom-of-kourion.e: In the Ionian Revolt, King Stasanor deserted to the Persians at the Battle of Salamis in 497 BCE. Later King Pasicrates aided Alexander at Tyre. The monarchy was abolished under Ptolemy I c. 312 BCE, and Kourion flourished as a Roman and early Christian city until earthquakes in the 4th century CE.
kingdom-of-kourion.re: Greek religion; cult of Apollo Hylates

kingdom-of-cyprus.t: Crusader kingdom of the Lusignan dynasty that ruled Cyprus for three centuries, the last Latin outpost in the Levant after the fall of Acre.
kingdom-of-cyprus.o: In 1192 Richard I sold Cyprus, recently taken from Isaac Komnenos and returned by the Templars, to Guy of Lusignan, the deposed king of Jerusalem. Guy settled Frankish knights on the island. His brother Aimery obtained a crown from the Emperor Henry VI and was crowned king in 1197.
kingdom-of-cyprus.r: A French-speaking Catholic nobility ruled a mostly Greek Orthodox population, using the laws of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and a High Court of barons. The Orthodox church was subordinated to Latin bishops. After the fall of Acre in 1291 Famagusta became a great entrepot for Italian merchants. Gothic cathedrals in Nicosia and Famagusta and the abbey of Bellapais survive. Peter I led a crusade that sacked Alexandria in 1365.
kingdom-of-cyprus.e: Genoa seized Famagusta in 1373, and a Mamluk invasion in 1426 captured King Janus and made the kingdom tributary to Egypt. James II married the Venetian Catherine Cornaro; after his death she ruled as queen until Venice forced her to abdicate in 1489, creating Venetian Cyprus.

kingdom-of-idalion.t: Inland Cypriot kingdom famous for the Idalion Tablet, a bronze contract recording how the city paid a doctor to treat the wounded during a siege.
kingdom-of-idalion.o: Idalion grew on the hills of central Cyprus, near the copper-bearing foothills of Troodos, in the early Iron Age. By the 7th century BCE it was a city-kingdom listed among Cypriot states paying tribute to the Assyrian king Esarhaddon. Its acropolis held sanctuaries of the goddesses later called Athena and Aphrodite.
kingdom-of-idalion.r: Idalion controlled copper production and fertile land. The Idalion Tablet, a bronze plaque of the early 5th century BCE written in the Cypriot syllabary, records that King Stasicypros and the city granted land to the physician Onasilos and his brothers for treating those wounded when 'the Medes and the Kitians' besieged the town.
kingdom-of-idalion.e: Idalion was conquered by the Phoenician Kingdom of Kition c. 450 BCE and lost its independence, Kition then ruling it with Phoenician administration. The town continued under Ptolemaic and Roman rule but declined.

kingdom-of-macedon.t: The Argead kingdom of northern Greece that Philip II turned into the dominant power of the Greek world, launching the conquests of his son Alexander.
kingdom-of-macedon.o: The Argead kings, who claimed descent from Temenos of Argos, built a kingdom in the plains of Lower Macedonia around Aigai, modern Vergina. Herodotus names Perdiccas I as founder in the 7th century BCE; later writers added an earlier Caranus, traditionally dated 808 BCE. The kingdom expanded over the Haliacmon and Axios plains.
kingdom-of-macedon.r: Macedon was a monarchy whose king ruled with a warrior aristocracy of Companions. It was a vassal of the Achaemenid Empire c. 512 to 479 BCE; Alexander I then courted Greek opinion. Archelaus I moved the capital to Pella c. 400 BCE and hosted Euripides. Timber, silver and horses supported it. Philip II, from 359 BCE, built a professional army with the long sarissa pike.
kingdom-of-macedon.e: Philip II took Amphipolis and the Chalcidice, defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE and founded the League of Corinth. His murder at Aigai in 336 BCE brought Alexander to the throne, opening the age of the Macedonian Empire.

kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.t: The Napoleonic kingdom of southern Italy under Joseph Bonaparte and Joachim Murat, which abolished feudalism in the south.
kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.o: After the Bourbon Kingdom of Naples joined the coalition against France, Napoleon sent an army in 1806. King Ferdinand IV fled to Sicily under British protection, and Napoleon made his brother Joseph Bonaparte king of Naples.
kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.r: Joseph abolished feudalism in 1806, closed monasteries and introduced French administration. In 1808 he became king of Spain and was succeeded by Joachim Murat, Napoleon's brother-in-law, who introduced the Napoleonic Code, built roads and fought brigandage in Calabria. The kingdom never controlled Sicily, which the Bourbons held with British help.
kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.e: Murat abandoned Napoleon in 1814, but in 1815 he declared war on Austria with the Rimini Proclamation calling for Italian independence. Defeated at Tolentino in May 1815, he fled; landing in Calabria in October, he was captured and shot. Ferdinand returned to Naples.

kingdom-of-dacia.t: Kingdom of the Dacians in the Carpathian basin, united by Burebista and defended by Decebalus against Trajan, whose conquest created Roman Dacia.
kingdom-of-dacia.o: About 82 BCE Burebista united the Getae and Dacian tribes, aided by the high priest Deceneus. He built a realm from the middle Danube to the Black Sea, defeating the Boii and Scordisci and taking Greek coastal cities such as Olbia and Apollonia.
kingdom-of-dacia.r: The heart of the kingdom lay in the Orăștie Mountains, where fortresses and sanctuaries ringed the capital, Sarmizegetusa Regia. Kings ruled with a priestly elite devoted to Zalmoxis. Gold and silver mining, iron working and trade with Rome supported the state. After Burebista's murder in 44 BCE the realm split, but Decebalus reunited it and defeated a Roman army at Tapae.
kingdom-of-dacia.e: Trajan's two Dacian Wars (101–102 and 105–106 CE) destroyed the kingdom; Sarmizegetusa fell and Decebalus killed himself in 106 CE. Most of the land became the province of Dacia, commemorated on Trajan's Column, and Dacian identity later became central to Romanian national history.

kingdom-of-viguera.t: A short-lived sub-kingdom in La Rioja, carved out of Pamplona for a royal younger son and soon folded back into the realm of Navarre.
kingdom-of-viguera.o: Around 970 King Sancho II Garcés of Pamplona, following the will of his father García Sánchez I, granted the Rioja lands around Viguera to his younger brother Ramiro Garcés with the title of king. The territory, recently won from the Muslims, guarded the upper Ebro and the approaches to Nájera.
kingdom-of-viguera.r: Viguera was an appanage rather than a fully independent state: its kings acknowledged the senior line in Pamplona and fought alongside it against the Caliphate of Córdoba. Ramiro is said to have died at the Battle of Torrevicente in 981. Charters show his sons Sancho Ramírez and García Ramírez styled as kings, though little else is recorded.
kingdom-of-viguera.e: After the line of Ramiro faded out in the early 11th century, Viguera was reabsorbed into the Kingdom of Navarre, by then under Sancho III the Great. It survives chiefly as a case study in how Iberian kings provided for younger sons with subordinate royal titles.

kingdom-of-provence.t: Short-lived Carolingian kingdom of the lower Rhône, carved out for the youngest son of Lothair I.
kingdom-of-provence.o: When Lothair I divided Middle Francia in 855, his youngest son Charles, still a boy, received Provence and the duchy of Lyon, stretching from the Mediterranean up the Rhône valley.
kingdom-of-provence.r: Charles suffered from epilepsy, and the kingdom was effectively run by Count Girart of Vienne, his guardian, who defended it against the ambitions of Charles the Bald and fought Viking raiders who had sailed up the Rhône. Vienne and Lyon were its main centres.
kingdom-of-provence.e: Charles died childless in 863, and his brothers Lothair II and the emperor Louis II divided the kingdom between them. The region later re-emerged as the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy under Boso in 879.

kamarina.t: Syracusan colony on Sicily's south coast, destroyed and refounded several times, whose restless history became a Greek proverb.
kamarina.o: Syracuse founded Kamarina around 598 BCE near the mouth of the Hipparis river, on the south-east coast of Sicily, to extend its reach towards the territory of Gela. The settlers laid out a regular town on a coastal hill beside a marsh.
kamarina.r: Kamarina repeatedly defied its mother city: it revolted around 553 BCE and was destroyed, was refounded by Hippocrates of Gela around 492 BCE, emptied again by Gelon in 484 BCE and refounded from Gela in 461 BCE. Pindar wrote odes for its Olympic victor Psaumis. The Greek proverb 'do not move Camarina', said to come from a disastrous draining of the marsh, warned against stirring up trouble.
kamarina.e: Its people evacuated before the Carthaginians in 405 BCE, and Timoleon resettled it in the 4th century. In 258 BCE, during the First Punic War, the Romans captured it and sold most inhabitants into slavery. The site, near Santa Croce Camerina, was excavated from the 19th century.

kingdom-of-ui-failge.t: Irish midland kingdom of the O'Connor Faly, which resisted English expansion from its bogland strongholds until the plantation of Offaly in 1556.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.o: The Uí Failge, 'descendants of Failge', claimed descent from Rus Failge, a son of the legendary Leinster king Cathair Mór. From the early medieval period they held a kingdom in the north-west of the Kingdom of Leinster, in what is now County Offaly, which takes its name from them. From the 11th century their rulers were the Ua Conchobair Failge, O'Connor Faly.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.r: Their territory of bog, esker and woodland was hard for invaders to penetrate. After the Anglo-Norman invasion the FitzGeralds of Kildare took their eastern lands, but the O'Connors Faly held the rest, raiding the Pale and taking protection payments known as black rent. Their stronghold at Daingean, set among bogs, was their main fortress in the 16th century.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.e: After Brian O'Connor Faly rebelled and surrendered in the 1540s, the English took Daingean. In 1556 the government of Mary I shired the kingdom as King's County, with Daingean renamed Philipstown, and planted it with English settlers, ending the kingdom.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-gwynedd.t: The most enduring Welsh kingdom, ruled from Aberffraw on Anglesey, whose princes led Welsh resistance until Edward I's conquest in 1283.
kingdom-of-gwynedd.o: Gwynedd arose in north-west Wales after Roman rule ended. Its dynasty traced descent from Cunedda, said to have come from Manaw Gododdin in the 5th century. By the 6th century it was a leading power under Maelgwn Gwynedd, whom Gildas denounced as Maglocunus, the dragon of the island, and its core lay in Snowdonia and the grain lands of Anglesey.
kingdom-of-gwynedd.r: Kings ruled from llysoedd, royal courts, with Aberffraw as the chief seat, governing through cantrefi and kin-based Welsh law. Cadwallon ap Cadfan killed Edwin of Northumbria in 633. Rhodri the Great, who died in 878, joined the Kingdom of Powys and Seisyllwg to Gwynedd. Later princes such as Owain Gwynedd and Llywelyn the Great built castles and charters, and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd won recognition as Prince of Wales by the Treaty of Montgomery in 1267.
kingdom-of-gwynedd.e: Edward I invaded in 1277 and again in 1282. Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was killed at Cilmeri in 1282, and his brother Dafydd was executed in 1283. The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 turned Gwynedd into English shires, guarded by castles such as Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech.

kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.t: The O'Neill kingdom of mid-Ulster, the most powerful Gaelic lordship of late medieval Ireland, whose last ruler led the Nine Years' War.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.o: Tir Eoghain, 'Eogan's land', descends from the Cenel nEogain, the northern Ui Neill kindred traced to Eogan, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. After the decline of the Mac Lochlainn line in the late 12th century, the O'Neills emerged as kings, ruling from Dungannon with inaugurations at Tullyhogue.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.r: The O'Neills dominated Ulster, taking tribute from lesser lords such as the O'Cahans and Maguires. Their power rested on cattle, a large army including Scottish gallowglasses, and a court of poets and lawyers. Conn Bacach O'Neill became Earl of Tyrone in 1542, but conflict with the crown continued under Shane O'Neill.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.e: Hugh O'Neill led the Nine Years' War against England, but defeat at Kinsale in 1601 forced his submission. He left in the Flight of the Earls in 1607, and Tyrone was confiscated for the Plantation of Ulster in the Kingdom of Ireland.

kingdom-of-scotland.t: The medieval and early modern kingdom of the Scots, forged from Pictland and Dal Riata, which kept its independence until the Union with England in 1707.
kingdom-of-scotland.o: Tradition dates the kingdom to Kenneth MacAlpin, who ruled the Picts from about 843. The Pictish and Gaelic realms merged into the kingdom of Alba by around 900, centred on Scone and Dunkeld. It expanded over Lothian, Strathclyde, and in 1266 the Western Isles from Norway.
kingdom-of-scotland.r: Scotland developed royal burghs, feudal lordship and a church of its own under David I. The Wars of Independence, with William Wallace and Robert the Bruce's victory at Bannockburn in 1314, secured independence. The Stewart monarchy followed in 1371, Edinburgh became the capital, and the Reformation of 1560 created a Presbyterian church.
kingdom-of-scotland.e: In 1603 James VI inherited England, joining the crowns. The Acts of Union of 1707 merged the Scottish and English parliaments into the Kingdom of Great Britain, though Scotland kept its own law, church and education.

kingdom-of-kition.t: Phoenician kingdom on Cyprus, founded by Tyre, that conquered its Greek neighbours Idalion and Tamassos and was the birthplace of Zeno the Stoic.
kingdom-of-kition.o: Kition, at modern Larnaca, was a Late Bronze Age copper-working town. In the 9th century BCE Phoenicians from Tyre settled there and built a great temple of Astarte on the ruins of an earlier sanctuary. Kition probably began as a Tyrian dependency, and in 707 BCE Sargon II of Assyria set up a stele there recording Cypriot submission.
kingdom-of-kition.r: From the early 5th century BCE an independent Phoenician dynasty ruled Kition, beginning with Baalmelek I, and it was loyal to the Achaemenid Empire. Kition conquered Idalion c. 450 BCE, its kings then styling themselves rulers of both, and Pumiyaton later bought Tamassos. Its harbour served Persian fleets, and its kings issued coins showing Heracles-Melqart.
kingdom-of-kition.e: Ptolemy I executed Pumiyaton and annexed the kingdom in 312 BCE. Kition continued as a Ptolemaic and Roman city; its most famous son, Zeno, founded Stoic philosophy at Athens.
kingdom-of-kition.re: Phoenician religion; cults of Astarte and Melqart

kingdom-of-ergyng.t: A small British kingdom in the Wye valley around the Roman town of Ariconium, whose name survives in Archenfield, a Welsh-speaking district of Herefordshire.
kingdom-of-ergyng.o: Ergyng emerged after Roman rule ended, its name derived from Ariconium, an iron-working town near Ross-on-Wye. It appears in the 6th and 7th centuries in the charters of the Book of Llandaff, which name local kings such as Peibio, associated in legend with the birth of Saint Dubricius.
kingdom-of-ergyng.r: Ergyng was a Christian British kingdom in which churches and monasteries, many linked to Dubricius, held land through royal grants. Its rulers were at times linked to the dynasties of Gwent and Glywysing. Little else is reliably known of its government.
kingdom-of-ergyng.e: From the 7th century the kingdom was absorbed by Gwent, and English settlement from Mercia advanced into the area. By the 10th century it was the district of Archenfield, under English lordship but still Welsh in law and speech; Domesday Book recorded its Welsh customs.

kingdom-of-france.t: The monarchy that grew from the Capetians' small domain around Paris into Europe's most populous and centralised state, ending with the Revolution.
kingdom-of-france.o: In 987 the magnates elected Hugh Capet, duke of the Franks, as king after the last Carolingian died. The early Capetians directly controlled only the Île-de-France and Orléans, while dukes and counts of Normandy, Aquitaine, Burgundy and Flanders were in practice independent.
kingdom-of-france.r: Kings slowly extended the royal domain by war, marriage and law: Philip II took Normandy in 1204, Louis IX became a model of Christian kingship, and the Valois survived the Hundred Years' War. After the Wars of Religion, Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598. Louis XIV built absolute rule at Versailles, and French language and culture dominated Europe.
kingdom-of-france.e: Debt and political crisis led Louis XVI to call the Estates-General in 1789, beginning the Revolution. The monarchy became constitutional in 1791 and was abolished in September 1792, replaced by the French First Republic; Louis XVI was executed in 1793.

kingdom-of-dublin.t: The Norse kingdom founded around Dublin's harbour, a hub of the Viking trade network that linked Ireland to Scandinavia, Britain and the slave markets.
kingdom-of-dublin.o: Vikings built a fortified base, the longphort, at Dublin in 841. From 853 the annals record Amlaib and later Imar, ancestors of a dynasty of kings who ruled both Dublin and, at times, the Kingdom of York. Expelled by the Irish in 902, they returned in 917.
kingdom-of-dublin.r: Dublin was a trading town of streets, houses and workshops, revealed by excavations at Wood Quay, dealing in slaves, silver, furs and craft goods. It minted coins from about 997. Its rulers converted to Christianity in the 10th century and Sitric Silkbeard founded Christ Church Cathedral around 1030. Irish kings often controlled it as a valuable prize.
kingdom-of-dublin.e: After defeat at Clontarf in 1014, Dublin was dominated by Irish overkings. In 1170 Strongbow and Diarmait Mac Murchada captured it, and in 1171 Henry II made it the capital of the Lordship of Ireland.
kingdom-of-dublin.re: Norse paganism; Christianity from the 10th century

kingdom-of-spain.t: Spain's present parliamentary monarchy, built through the peaceful transition from Franco's dictatorship to democracy.
kingdom-of-spain.o: Two days after Franco's death, Juan Carlos I was proclaimed king on 22 November 1975, ending Francoist Spain. With Prime Minister Adolfo Suárez he dismantled the dictatorship: the Law for Political Reform of 1976, free elections in June 1977 and the Constitution of 1978, approved by referendum.
kingdom-of-spain.r: Spain became a parliamentary monarchy divided into 17 autonomous communities, recognising Catalan, Basque and Galician identities. The king's stand against the coup attempt of 23 February 1981 secured democracy. Felipe González's Socialists governed from 1982 to 1996, joining NATO and the European Economic Community in 1986. The 1992 Barcelona Olympics and Seville Expo marked modernisation.
kingdom-of-spain.e: Spain remains a parliamentary monarchy. ETA declared an end to violence in 2011, Felipe VI succeeded his father in 2014, and the Catalan independence crisis of 2017 tested the constitutional order.

kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.t: The Alpine kingdom of the Welf dynasty, founded at Saint-Maurice in 888, which later absorbed Provence to form the Kingdom of Arles.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.o: After the deposition of Emperor Charles the Fat in 888, the Welf noble Rudolf, margrave of Transjurane Burgundy, had himself crowned king at the abbey of Saint-Maurice d'Agaune. His kingdom covered western Switzerland, the Jura and parts of Franche-Comté, and he held it against the East Frankish king Arnulf.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.r: The kings controlled the Great St Bernard pass and relied on rich abbeys such as Saint-Maurice and on alliances with local bishops at Lausanne, Geneva and Sion. Rudolf II was defeated by Swabia at Winterthur in 919, then reached for the Italian crown in the 920s before trading those claims for Provence.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.e: Around 933 Rudolf II obtained Lower Burgundy from Hugh of Arles, merging the two realms into the Kingdom of Arles. His son Conrad the Peaceful ruled the united kingdom under strong Ottonian influence, and in 1032 it passed to the Holy Roman Empire.

kingdom-of-leon.t: The Christian kingdom that succeeded Asturias in 910, claimed Visigothic heritage and held the first European parliament with townsmen in 1188.
kingdom-of-leon.o: In 910 the sons of Alfonso III of Asturias divided his realm, García I taking León. In 914 Ordoño II made the city of León the royal seat, and the kingdom took its name from it, incorporating Asturias and Galicia and the newly resettled lands of the Douro plain.
kingdom-of-leon.r: The Leonese kings claimed to restore the Visigothic monarchy, some styling themselves emperor. Ramiro II beat Abd al-Rahman III at Simancas in 939, though Almanzor later sacked León and Santiago. Alfonso V's fuero of 1017 regulated the city, and Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085. Alfonso IX summoned the Cortes of León in 1188, with representatives of towns alongside nobles and clergy.
kingdom-of-leon.e: León was united with Castile under Ferdinand I and his successors, separated again from 1157, and definitively joined with Castile in 1230 under Ferdinand III, forming the Crown of Castile.

kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.t: The largest pre-unification Italian state, the Bourbon kingdom of Naples and Sicily, overthrown by Garibaldi's Thousand in 1860.
kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.o: After the Congress of Vienna restored him, Ferdinand IV of Naples and III of Sicily merged the Kingdom of Naples and the Kingdom of Sicily in December 1816, becoming Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies, with Naples as capital.
kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.r: The kingdom was an absolute monarchy that put down revolts in 1820 and 1848; Sicilians resented losing their autonomy. Ferdinand II opened Italy's first railway, from Naples to Portici, in 1839 and built a strong navy, but his harsh repression earned him the nickname King Bomba. The south remained largely rural, with powerful landowners and widespread poverty.
kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.e: In 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand conquered Sicily and Naples. Francis II held out at Gaeta until February 1861, and the kingdom was annexed to the new Kingdom of Italy.

kingdom-of-the-picts.t: Early medieval kingdom of northern and eastern Scotland, known for its carved symbol stones, which merged with the Gaels to form the kingdom of Alba.
kingdom-of-the-picts.o: The Picts are first named in a Roman panegyric of 297 as enemies of Britain alongside the Irish. The name, Latin for 'painted people', was applied to the peoples north of the Forth, descendants of the Caledonii, Maeatae and other Iron Age groups. Over the following centuries their many districts were drawn together under powerful over-kings.
kingdom-of-the-picts.r: The Picts left few written records but carved distinctive symbol stones with combs, mirrors, crescents and animals, later combined with Christian crosses. Kings such as Bridei son of Maelchon, visited by Columba in the 560s, ruled through regional lords. Bridei son of Beli defeated the Northumbrians at Dun Nechtain in 685, and Óengus son of Fergus dominated northern Britain in the 8th century. Christianity spread from Iona and Northumbria.
kingdom-of-the-picts.e: Viking attacks in the 9th century devastated the Pictish elite, notably in a great defeat in 839. Cináed mac Ailpín, a king of Gaelic descent, took power around 843, and by about 900 Pictland had become the Gaelic-speaking kingdom of Alba, the core of medieval Scotland.
kingdom-of-the-picts.re: Celtic polytheism; Christianity from the 6th century

kingdom-of-maroboduus.t: The first large Germanic kingdom known by name, built in Bohemia by Maroboduus, who drilled an army on Roman lines and alarmed Augustus.
kingdom-of-maroboduus.o: Maroboduus, a Marcomannic noble who had spent his youth in Rome, led his people from the Main region into Bohemia around 9 BCE to escape Roman offensives. There he subjected neighbouring peoples, including the Quadi, Lugii, Semnones and Langobardi, building a realm that stretched from the Danube to the Elbe and beyond.
kingdom-of-maroboduus.r: Velleius Paterculus describes a centralised monarchy with a standing army of about 70,000 foot and 4,000 horse trained in Roman fashion, and a royal seat called Marobudum. Roman merchants lived there. Augustus planned to crush him in 6 CE with twelve legions, but the Pannonian revolt forced a treaty recognising Maroboduus as a friend of Rome.
kingdom-of-maroboduus.e: Maroboduus stayed neutral when Arminius destroyed Varus' legions in 9, and in 17 Arminius defeated him; the Semnones and Langobardi deserted. In 19 the Gothic exile Catualda seized his capital, and Maroboduus fled to Roman territory, dying in Ravenna in 37. Rome then created the client Kingdom of Vannius.

kingdom-of-dyfed.t: South-west Welsh kingdom ruled by a dynasty of Irish descent, home of St Davids, which became the core of Deheubarth under Hywel Dda.
kingdom-of-dyfed.o: Dyfed grew from the Roman civitas of the Demetae after Roman rule ended around 410. Irish settlers crossed to the region in the 4th and 5th centuries, and its royal line traced descent from the Déisi of Ireland, a link supported by the many ogham-inscribed stones of the area.
kingdom-of-dyfed.r: In the 6th century Gildas denounced its king Vortiporius as tyrant of the Demetae, and a memorial stone at Castell Dwyran bearing his name in Latin and ogham may be his. The monastery of St Davids, founded by Dewi Sant, became the leading church of Wales. Asser records that its king Hyfaidd ap Bleddri submitted to Alfred of Wessex in the 880s to escape pressure from Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-dyfed.e: After Llywarch ap Hyfaidd died around 904, his daughter Elen married Hywel Dda of Seisyllwg, who took over Dyfed. Hywel joined the two realms to form the kingdom of Deheubarth, and Dyfed survived as a region and, much later, as a county name.

kingdom-of-naples.t: The southern Italian kingdom ruled from Naples for five centuries by Angevins, Aragonese, Spanish viceroys and Bourbons.
kingdom-of-naples.o: The Sicilian Vespers of 1282 drove Charles of Anjou from Sicily, leaving him only the mainland part of the Kingdom of Sicily. He and his heirs kept calling themselves kings of Sicily but ruled from Naples, which became the capital of a separate kingdom.
kingdom-of-naples.r: Robert the Wise made Naples a cultural centre, hosting Petrarch and Giotto. Alfonso V of Aragon conquered the kingdom in 1442. After French invasions, Spain ruled it from 1504 through viceroys, making Naples one of Europe's largest cities. A powerful baronage, heavy taxes and the Masaniello revolt of 1647 marked this period. Austria took the kingdom in 1707, and in 1734 Charles of Bourbon made it independent again.
kingdom-of-naples.e: Napoleon's armies drove out the Bourbons in 1806, creating the Kingdom of Naples (1806–1815). Ferdinand IV returned in 1815 and in 1816 united Naples and Sicily as the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

kingdom-of-aquitaine.t: Carolingian sub-kingdom of south-western Francia, created by Charlemagne for his son Louis the Pious.
kingdom-of-aquitaine.o: After crushing the last independent dukes of the Early Duchy of Aquitaine, Charlemagne made Aquitaine a kingdom for his three-year-old son Louis, crowned by the pope in Rome in 781. It reached from the Loire to the Pyrenees and was meant to secure the frontier against Al-Andalus.
kingdom-of-aquitaine.r: Louis governed with Frankish counts and advisers, reformed monasteries with Benedict of Aniane and led campaigns into Spain, taking Barcelona in 801. Royal residences included Toulouse, Poitiers and Chasseneuil. After he became emperor in 814 the kingdom passed to his son Pepin I.
kingdom-of-aquitaine.e: After Pepin I died in 838, his son Pepin II fought a long war against his uncle Charles the Bald of West Francia. Charles installed his own sons, Charles the Child and Louis the Stammerer, and when Louis succeeded to West Francia in 877 the kingdom merged into it.

kingdom-of-england.t: The medieval and early modern kingdom unified by Aethelstan, transformed by the Norman Conquest and joined with Scotland in 1707.
kingdom-of-england.o: In 927 Aethelstan took York and received the submission of the northern rulers, completing the work of the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons. Viking kings briefly regained York until 954, and Danish kings Cnut and his sons ruled England from 1016 to 1042.
kingdom-of-england.r: Late Anglo-Saxon England had shires, a strong coinage and royal writs. After William the Conqueror's victory at Hastings in 1066, Norman lords, Domesday Book and a French-speaking elite reshaped society. Magna Carta in 1215, the growth of Parliament and common law, the wool trade and the Reformation under Henry VIII defined later centuries.
kingdom-of-england.e: England annexed Wales between 1283 and 1543 and ruled the Lordship of Ireland. James VI of Scotland inherited the crown in 1603, and after the Civil War and the Commonwealth of England, the Acts of Union of 1707 created the Kingdom of Great Britain.

kingdom-of-the-geats.t: The kingdom or kingdoms of the Geats in southern Sweden's Götaland, the people of Beowulf, later merged with the Svear to form Sweden.
kingdom-of-the-geats.o: Ptolemy and Jordanes mention Gautoi and Gautigoths in southern Scandinavia, and the Old English poem Beowulf makes the Geats and their king Hygelac its heroes. Hygelac's raid on Frisia, recorded by Gregory of Tours around 520, is one of the few datable events. Their heartland lay in Västergötland and Östergötland, around lakes Vänern and Vättern.
kingdom-of-the-geats.r: Whether the Geats formed one kingdom or several regional lordships is uncertain. Each land kept its own assembly and laws, later written down as the Västgötalagen. Society was based on farming, ironworking and a warrior aristocracy, and the region kept close ties with Denmark across the Kattegat.
kingdom-of-the-geats.e: Around 1000 the Geats came under the kings of the Svear, and Olof Skötkonung, traditionally baptised at Husaby in Västergötland, ruled both peoples. Götaland remained a distinct part of the Kingdom of Sweden, with its own lawmen, and its people sometimes elected rival kings into the 12th century.

kingdom-of-osraige.t: Irish kingdom between Leinster and Munster, centred on Kilkenny, whose Mac Giolla Phádraig rulers survived as lords until the Tudor surrender of 1541.
kingdom-of-osraige.o: Osraige emerged in early medieval Ireland as the kingdom of a people living in the valleys of the Nore and its tributaries, in modern County Kilkenny and south Laois. Its kings traced descent from ancestors distinct from both the Laigin and the Eóganachta, and the kingdom stood between the Kingdom of Leinster and the Kingdom of Munster, usually as a tributary of Munster.
kingdom-of-osraige.r: The monasteries of Saighir, linked with St Ciarán, and later Aghaboe and Kilkenny, where St Canice is honoured, were centres of learning and gave their names to the diocese of Ossory. Cerball mac Dúnlainge, who died in 888, made Osraige a major power by fighting and allying with Viking leaders. His descendants, the Mac Giolla Phádraig, briefly held the kingship of Leinster under Donnchad mac Gilla Pátraic in the 1030s.
kingdom-of-osraige.e: After the Anglo-Norman invasion of 1169, Kilkenny became the seat of English lords, and the Mac Giolla Phádraig held only Upper Ossory. In 1541 their chief, Brian, surrendered his lands to Henry VIII and received them back as Baron of Upper Ossory, ending the kingdom.

kingdom-of-cornwall.t: The last surviving British kingdom of the south-west peninsula, which held out against Wessex until the 9th and 10th centuries.
kingdom-of-cornwall.o: Cornwall emerged as a separate British kingdom as the larger kingdom of Dumnonia shrank under West Saxon pressure. By the early 8th century Wessex had taken Devon, and the British realm beyond the Tamar became known as Kernow or Cornwall. Its kings are poorly recorded; Geraint fought Ine of Wessex around 710.
kingdom-of-cornwall.r: Cornwall kept its Brittonic language, saints' cults and links with Wales and Brittany. Tin mining and sea trade continued from Roman times. A defeat of a combined Cornish and Viking army at Hingston Down in 838 shows its kings still resisting the Kingdom of Wessex. The Annales Cambriae record the drowning of King Dungarth in 875.
kingdom-of-cornwall.e: Cornwall was brought under English control by the 9th century, and Aethelstan fixed the Tamar as the boundary around 936. It became part of the Kingdom of England, while the Cornish language survived into the 18th century.

kingdom-of-fermanagh.t: The Maguire lordship around Lough Erne, a Gaelic lordship of islands and churches whose last chief joined the Flight of the Earls.
kingdom-of-fermanagh.o: The Maguires rose in Fermanagh in the 13th century, with Donn Mor Maguire recognised as king in 1264. They displaced earlier rulers and became vassals of the O'Neills of the Kingdom of Tir Eoghain.
kingdom-of-fermanagh.r: Fermanagh was organised around Lough Erne, with islands, crannogs and monasteries such as Devenish. The Maguires built Enniskillen Castle in the 15th century. Their learned families compiled the Annals of Ulster on Belle Isle under Cathal Mac Maghnusa. Their economy rested on cattle and fishing.
kingdom-of-fermanagh.e: Hugh Maguire fought with Hugh O'Neill in the Nine Years' War and died in 1600. His brother Cuchonnacht left with the Flight of the Earls in 1607. Fermanagh was then planted with English and Scottish settlers, and Enniskillen became a Protestant garrison town.

kingdom-of-lotharingia.t: Northern share of Middle Francia, named after its king Lothair II, whose name survives in Lorraine.
kingdom-of-lotharingia.o: At the Treaty of Prüm in 855 Lothair I left the northern part of Middle Francia, from Frisia through the Low Countries and the Rhineland to the Vosges, to his son Lothair II. The kingdom took its name from him as the realm of Lothair.
kingdom-of-lotharingia.r: It held the old Carolingian heartland around Aachen, Metz, Trier and Cologne, with wealthy abbeys and episcopal cities. Lothair II's reign was dominated by his attempt to divorce his childless wife Teutberga and marry Waldrada, which Pope Nicholas I blocked, leaving him without a legitimate heir.
kingdom-of-lotharingia.e: After Lothair II died in 869 his uncles divided the kingdom at Meerssen in 870, and in 880 all of it passed to East Francia. Arnulf of Carinthia made his son Zwentibold king in 895, but he was killed in 900, and the land became the Duchy of Lotharingia.

kingdom-of-glywysing.t: Kingdom of south-east Wales between the Usk and the Tawe, home of the great monasteries of Llantwit and Llancarfan, which became Morgannwg.
kingdom-of-glywysing.o: Glywysing took its name from Glywys, a legendary 5th-century king whose descendants, according to the Lives of the Welsh saints, included St Cadoc. It grew from the post-Roman communities of the Glamorgan lowlands, once the territory of the Silures, and was often joined with the neighbouring Kingdom of Gwent under a single dynasty.
kingdom-of-glywysing.r: The Llandaff charters, a collection of land grants, show a society of kings, churchmen and landowners trading estates and gifts. Meurig ap Tewdrig and his descendants ruled across Glywysing and Gwent from the 7th century. The monasteries of Llantwit Major, founded by St Illtud, and Llancarfan, founded by St Cadoc, were leading centres of learning. Asser says Hywel ap Rhys submitted to Alfred.
kingdom-of-glywysing.e: In the 10th century Morgan Hen ruled both Glywysing and Gwent, and from around 942 his combined realm became known as Morgannwg, from which the name Glamorgan derives. The region later fell to the Normans under Robert Fitzhamon in the 1090s.

kingdom-of-italy.t: The united Italian monarchy of the House of Savoy, which completed unification, fought two world wars and fell to a referendum in 1946.
kingdom-of-italy.o: On 17 March 1861 the parliament in Turin proclaimed Victor Emmanuel II of the Kingdom of Sardinia king of Italy, after the annexation of Lombardy, central Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. Venetia was added in 1866 and Rome taken from the Papal States in 1870.
kingdom-of-italy.r: The capital moved from Turin to Florence in 1865 and to Rome in 1871. Under the Statuto Albertino, liberal governments led by Agostino Depretis, Francesco Crispi and Giovanni Giolitti industrialised the north while millions emigrated. Italy entered the First World War in 1915. Benito Mussolini took power in 1922, built a Fascist dictatorship, signed the Lateran Treaty in 1929, conquered Ethiopia in 1936 and allied with Nazi Germany.
kingdom-of-italy.e: Defeat led the king to dismiss Mussolini in 1943 and sign an armistice with the Allies. On 2 June 1946 a referendum abolished the monarchy, creating the Italian Republic.

kingdom-of-soloi.t: Cypriot kingdom on Morphou Bay, said to have taken its name from the Athenian lawgiver Solon, who advised its king.
kingdom-of-soloi.o: Soloi lay on the bay of Morphou in north-western Cyprus, near the copper mines of Skouriotissa. Founded in the early Iron Age, it was a city-kingdom by the 7th century BCE. Plutarch tells that King Philocyprus moved the city to a better site on Solon's advice and named it after him.
kingdom-of-soloi.r: Soloi grew rich on copper and farmland. Its king Aristocyprus fell fighting the Persians at Salamis in 497 BCE, after which Soloi endured a five-month siege. The palace of Vouni on a nearby hill, built in the 5th century BCE, may have been used to watch over Soloi. King Pasicrates aided Alexander at Tyre in 332 BCE.
kingdom-of-soloi.e: Its last king, Eunostos, married Eirene, daughter of Ptolemy I, and the kingdom was absorbed into Ptolemaic Cyprus c. 312 BCE. Soloi remained a city into Roman and early Christian times.
